title: Customer Profitability Analysis: Revenue, Cost to Serve and Decisions
seoTitle: Customer Profitability: Formula & Example
description: Measure customer profit with a reconciled cost-to-serve example. Separate avoidable costs, shared overhead and cash timing before changing an account.
metaDescription: Measure customer profit with a reconciled cost-to-serve example. Separate avoidable costs, shared overhead and cash timing before changing an account.
opening: Customer profitability analysis compares a customer’s net revenue with the direct and shared costs of serving that customer during the same period. Show contribution and allocated profit separately before deciding whether a relationship should change.
alt: Business owner comparing three customer folders with delivery, support and invoice records.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
Customer profitability analysis compares a customer’s net revenue with the direct and shared costs of serving that customer during the same period. Show contribution and allocated profit separately before deciding whether a relationship should change.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Define the period and the cost boundary

Start with a customer-month, quarter or year. Use earned revenue after discounts, credits and returns for that period. Keep collections in a separate dated view: an unpaid invoice can create accounting revenue without available cash. Define whether your result includes acquisition spending, account support, general overhead and owner work.

Customer contribution = net revenue − directly traceable delivery and service costs. Then subtract assigned shared service costs to obtain the specifically defined allocated result. Label the boundary; do not call a partially costed margin company net income. A customer’s lifetime value uses a different horizon and needs retention assumptions.

Reconcile three customers to the business total

Fictional monthly customer ledger
MeasureCustomer ACustomer BCustomer CTotal
Net revenue$6,000$4,000$2,000$12,000
Direct delivery$2,400$2,000$1,200$5,600
Support hours10203060
Support at $40/hour$400$800$1,200$2,400
Contribution after support$3,200$1,200−$400$4,000
General overhead allocated$900$600$300$1,800
Allocated result$2,300$600−$700$2,200

The support pool is $2,400 divided by 60 practical support hours, giving $40 per hour. General overhead is allocated by revenue only to reconcile the remaining $1,800. Its allocation is a reporting choice, not evidence that the cash disappears when a customer leaves. Total revenue of $12,000 less $5,600 delivery, $2,400 support and $1,800 overhead equals $2,200.

Choose drivers that explain actual work

Use order lines for processing, support time for assistance, shipments for dispatch and documented collection effort for chasing overdue balances. Do not allocate every pool by sales simply because sales is available. Record the pool amount, source ledger, included activity, denominator and each customer’s usage. The sum of allocations must equal the amount assigned; idle capacity or unassigned overhead should remain visible.

For acquisition cost, choose and disclose a treatment. Expensing all campaign spend in the acquisition month may be useful for that month’s result; spreading it over an assumed relationship produces a different managerial measure. Neither choice should silently mix lifetime acquisition cost with one month’s revenue.

Test an action instead of automatically dropping the customer

Customer C looks loss-making after allocation. Suppose a standard-order policy removes ten support hours. At the chosen $40 rate, the ledger shows $400 less assigned support and a zero contribution after support. But if salaried staff are still paid, near-term cash does not improve by $400. Instead, released hours may let the same team serve better work.

Before repricing or exiting, list contract commitments, collection risk, rework, spare capacity and costs genuinely avoided. Compare a scoped service level, paid rush requests, minimum order or staged price change with the current account. A negative allocated result is a reason to investigate, not an automatic customer termination rule.

Build a monthly account review that can be audited

  1. Reconcile customer net revenue to the sales ledger.
  2. Trace delivery, refunds and customer-specific effort from source records.
  3. Allocate only identified service pools using documented drivers.
  4. Show unassigned overhead and reconcile the complete business result.
  5. Choose an action, name an owner and review the next period’s actuals.

Use the agency client profitability guide for a service-account application, and the cleaning contract profit calculator for a contract-specific cost boundary. Check those records against the broader contribution income statement.

faq.q: Is a high-revenue customer always profitable?
faq.a: No. Discounts, delivery effort, exceptions, support and collection work can consume the apparent margin. Compare consistently costed results for the same period.

faq.q: Should shared overhead determine whether to drop a customer?
faq.a: Not by itself. Test avoidable costs and released capacity; allocated overhead may remain after the account leaves.

faq.q: Which cost driver should I use?
faq.a: Choose a documented measure that explains the activity, such as support hours or shipments. Reconcile the allocated pool and show any unassigned cost.

faq.q: Can profit be positive while collections are late?
faq.a: Yes. Accrual revenue and customer contribution do not establish available cash. Track invoice due dates and receipts separately.

title: ROAS vs ROI: Follow One Campaign from Revenue to Profit
seoTitle: ROAS vs ROI: Costs & Worked Example
description: Compare ROAS and ROI using one campaign ledger. Include refunds, product costs and creative fees, and state the investment denominator before comparing returns.
metaDescription: Compare ROAS and ROI using one campaign ledger. Include refunds, product costs and creative fees, and state the investment denominator before comparing returns.
opening: ROAS divides attributed conversion revenue by ad spend. ROI compares a defined net profit with a defined investment cost. A high ROAS can coexist with a loss when product, fulfillment, refunds and campaign costs absorb the revenue.
alt: Marketer comparing attributed advertising revenue with a separate product-cost and campaign-profit ledger.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
ROAS divides attributed conversion revenue by ad spend. ROI compares a defined net profit with a defined investment cost. A high ROAS can coexist with a loss when product, fulfillment, refunds and campaign costs absorb the revenue.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Write both formulas and state what each includes

ROAS = attributed conversion revenue ÷ advertising spend. A 4× result means $4 attributed revenue for each $1 of media spend; it is not $4 profit. Where a platform tracks non-revenue conversion value, call the metric conversion-value ROAS rather than cash sales.

ROI = net return ÷ defined investment cost × 100%. Net return subtracts the costs included in that definition. Some teams report campaign profit divided by media/marketing investment; others divide by all included costs. Both can be interpretable, but only if the numerator and denominator are explicit and comparable.

Work through one completed campaign

Original fictional campaign, one matched reporting window
Ledger itemAmountTreatment
Net attributed revenue$12,000After credits/returns in this example
Ad spend$3,000Media only
Product costs$5,400Cost of fulfilled sales
Fulfillment and transaction fees$1,800Additional sale-linked costs
Creative and campaign support$1,200Separate from media
Included total cost$11,400Sum of all four cost lines
Profit after included costs$600$12,000 − $11,400

ROAS is $12,000 ÷ $3,000 = 4×, or 400%. Total-cost ROI is $600 ÷ $11,400 = 5.26%. A separately labelled marketing-investment return is $600 ÷ ($3,000 + $1,200) = 14.29%. The different percentages do not conflict: their cost bases differ. The case excludes general company overhead, interest and tax, so $600 is not represented as company net income.

Find the threshold implied by this exact ledger

Product and fulfillment costs total $7,200, or 60% of net revenue. The pre-marketing contribution ratio is 40%. Ignoring the separate creative/support cost, media-only break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5×. Including $1,200 creative/support and holding $3,000 media spend fixed requires revenue of ($3,000 + $1,200) ÷ 0.40 = $10,500, or 3.5× media ROAS.

This threshold assumes a stable cost ratio, net revenue definition and campaign support budget. If returns, order mix or fulfillment rates change, recalculate. Use the existing break-even ROAS calculator and its formula explanation for the threshold task rather than creating a second ROAS tool.

Keep the sales result constant and change the economics

If fulfillment and fees increase by $900, profit falls from $600 to −$300 while ROAS remains 4×. Included costs become $12,300 and total-cost ROI becomes −2.44%. That is why creative changes that raise revenue can still damage profit when they also increase discounts, returns or expensive deliveries.

Track net revenue, contribution before media, campaign profit and cash settlement together. Compare cohorts only after a consistent conversion/return window. An order reported today may be returned later, and a payment processor can settle cash on another date.

Do not turn attribution into proof of incremental sales

Attributed conversions follow a platform’s measurement model. They do not establish how many sales would have happened without advertising. Separate branded/returning-customer attribution from a documented incrementality test. Do not combine overlapping platform revenue totals as though every order were unique.

Before increasing spend, verify currency, revenue events, refunds, attribution windows, cost imports and the investment definition. Review ecommerce unit economics and the business ROI calculator when the decision includes more than advertising.

faq.q: Is 400% ROAS the same as 400% ROI?
faq.a: No. A 400% ROAS is 4× attributed value divided by media spend. ROI uses net return and a separately defined investment denominator.

faq.q: Which result should I use for scaling?
faq.a: Review contribution and campaign profit, attribution quality, capacity and cash timing together. A revenue ratio alone does not establish profitable incremental growth.

faq.q: Should refunds change the revenue input?
faq.a: Use a consistently defined net revenue measure and a matched return window. Do not subtract a refund again if it is already netted in the input.

faq.q: Does reported ROAS prove advertising caused the sales?
faq.a: No. Attribution assigns credit under a model. Incrementality requires evidence about sales that would not have happened without the campaign.

title: Sales Forecast Formula: Build a Capacity-Checked Small-Business Plan
seoTitle: Sales Forecast Formula & Business Template
description: Build a sales forecast from units, price and customer evidence. Check capacity, separate bookings from cash and compare scenarios with an editable worksheet.
metaDescription: Build a sales forecast from units, price and customer evidence. Check capacity, separate bookings from cash and compare scenarios with an editable worksheet.
opening: A practical sales forecast sums expected units multiplied by net selling price for each offer and period. Build the unit assumptions from customer evidence, check delivery capacity, and keep revenue recognition and collection dates separate.
alt: Business owner building a sales plan from order cards, a calendar and a qualified pipeline beside product samples.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
A practical sales forecast sums expected units multiplied by net selling price for each offer and period. Build the unit assumptions from customer evidence, check delivery capacity, and keep revenue recognition and collection dates separate.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Choose a method that matches the evidence you have

For repeat services, begin with opening customers, expected completed work and known renewals. For a product line, use expected sold units and net unit prices. For a qualified pipeline, sum opportunity value multiplied by a documented close probability for the relevant period. Historical growth can supply a baseline, but unexplained percentage growth is not customer evidence.

Forecast sales = Σ(expected units × net unit price). A weighted pipeline is an expectation across uncertain outcomes, not a promise that a fractional contract will close. Do not add the same sale again when it appears in both a customer schedule and the pipeline.

A target of 60 recurring jobs and 12 one-off jobs would need 168 hours, so demand or sales ambition alone cannot support it. Keep worker-hours distinct from elapsed clock hours when several people attend a job.

The upside is a demand case, not an executable delivery forecast. It needs 32 more productive hours, a revised offer mix or rescheduling. If overtime or contractors add cost, update contribution and cash along with sales. If cancellations are already incorporated in completed-job assumptions, do not subtract them a second time.

Separate signed work, delivered revenue and cash received

A signed $3,000 agreement in November might be delivered in December and collected in January. Keep separate columns for signed bookings, the revenue period under the applicable accounting treatment, and the expected receipt date. The illustrative tables use completed service work as the sales basis; they are not tax-method guidance.

Once sales are built, send dated receipts into the cash-flow forecast. Use the rolling forecast guide to update the horizon as actual months close. These are linked tasks, not interchangeable templates.

Measure forecast error and improve the assumptions

Freeze a dated forecast version before the month begins. Compare actual units, net price, mix, cancellations and timing against that version. If actual revenue is $10,200 against $10,800, the dollar error is −$600 and the shortfall versus forecast is 5.56%. This stated denominator is forecast revenue; a metric using actual revenue would produce a different percentage.

Review persistent bias rather than rewriting the old forecast to match actuals. For a new business, replace weak assumptions with paid pilots, signed scope, customer interviews and observed conversion rates as evidence accumulates. Retain the source date and owner of each assumption in the business plan evidence register.

faq.q: Can a sales target be used as a forecast?
faq.a: A target states an ambition. A forecast estimates an outcome from stated evidence and assumptions. Keep both visible rather than treating the target as proof.

faq.q: Does the forecast show cash available?
faq.a: Not by itself. Put delivery, invoice and collection dates into a separate dated cash schedule.

faq.q: How should I handle an upside above capacity?
faq.a: Label it a demand scenario and calculate the additional worker-hours or other constrained resources before treating it as deliverable revenue.

faq.q: What error denominator does the example use?
faq.a: It divides the revenue shortfall by forecast revenue. State the denominator because using actual revenue produces another percentage.

title: Cost Volume Profit Analysis: Break-Even, Target Profit and Capacity
seoTitle: Cost Volume Profit Analysis: Scenarios
description: Test price, costs, volume, sales mix and capacity with CVP analysis. Reconcile break-even and target profit before accepting a higher fixed-cost commitment.
metaDescription: Test price, costs, volume, sales mix and capacity with CVP analysis. Reconcile break-even and target profit before accepting a higher fixed-cost commitment.
opening: Cost-volume-profit analysis tests how price, variable costs, fixed costs and sold volume combine to produce operating profit. Break-even is its zero-profit case; the useful business decision also checks demand, product mix and the capacity range.
alt: Product-business manager reviewing price, variable materials and fixed overhead beside a packaging workbench.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
Cost-volume-profit analysis tests how price, variable costs, fixed costs and sold volume combine to produce operating profit. Break-even is its zero-profit case; the useful business decision also checks demand, product mix and the capacity range.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Start with one consistent unit and cost boundary

Operating profit = units × (net price − variable cost per unit) − fixed operating costs. Contribution per unit is net price less variable cost. The contribution ratio divides that contribution by price. Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by positive unit contribution. Required units for a profit target equal (fixed costs + target operating profit) divided by unit contribution.

If contribution is zero or negative, selling more of the unchanged offer does not cover positive fixed costs. Keep every amount in the same period and currency. Owner wages included in fixed costs must not be added again as a separate profit goal. Drawings and financing require separate cash treatment.

Reconcile the profit at several volumes

Original fictional monthly case: $120 price, $72 variable cost, $9,600 fixed costs
Sold unitsSalesVariable costContributionOperating profit
150$18,000$10,800$7,200−$2,400
200$24,000$14,400$9,600$0
250$30,000$18,000$12,000$2,400
300$36,000$21,600$14,400$4,800

Unit contribution is $48, the contribution ratio is 40%, and exact break-even is 200 units or $24,000. A $4,800 operating-profit target requires 300 units. A $5,000 target would require 304.1667 units mathematically; 305 whole units produce $5,040 profit under the unchanged assumptions.

Check the capacity step before trusting the target

Suppose existing resources can deliver only 260 units. Selling 300 requires another $2,400 monthly capacity commitment. The fixed-cost base becomes $12,000 and 300 units now produce $2,400, not $4,800. To recover the original $4,800 target at the same price and variable rate requires 350 units. That second target also needs its own capacity and demand check.

A discounted price of $110 leaves only $38 contribution at the original $72 variable rate. With the original $9,600 fixed base, break-even becomes 252.6316 exact units, or 253 whole units. These comparisons isolate a changed assumption; combining them without rebuilding the full model would misstate the answer.

A sales mix changes what an average unit means

For two offers contributing $40 and $70 per unit, a 3:2 unit mix creates a five-unit bundle with $260 contribution. At $10,400 fixed cost, break-even is 40 bundles: 120 units of the first offer and 80 of the second. The weighted unit contribution is $52. If the mix changes, that average no longer applies.

Use the existing multiple-product break-even guide for the mix calculation. The contribution income statement reconciles cost behavior; the target-profit guide owns the detailed units-and-sales task.

Know when the straight-line model stops answering the question

Simple CVP assumes stable price and variable cost per unit, a relevant fixed-cost range, meaningful cost classification and a stated mix. Inventory changes, capacity tiers, waste, payment fees and channel commissions can require a more detailed model. Profit is not available cash: collection delays, inventory purchases, debt principal and capital expenditure must also be scheduled.

Use flexible budget variance analysis to compare actual performance at actual volume rather than blaming a revenue shortfall on cost control. Treat a feasible profit target as a plan to test, not proof that buyers will order it.

faq.q: Is CVP the same as break-even analysis?
faq.a: Break-even is the zero-profit case within CVP. CVP also compares target profits and changes in volume, price, costs and mix.

faq.q: Why can a correct target still fail?
faq.a: It may exceed capacity, rely on unsupported demand or cross a fixed-cost step. A profit model also does not establish cash availability.

faq.q: What if contribution per unit is negative?
faq.a: With the same price and variable rate, additional units deepen the contribution shortfall. Resolve the economics before dividing fixed costs by contribution.

faq.q: Why does the product mix matter?
faq.a: Each offer can contribute a different amount. The weighted contribution is valid only for the stated mix and cost range.

title: Cost per Hire vs Employee Cost: Two Different Budgets
seoTitle: Cost per Hire vs Employee Cost: Example
description: Calculate recruiting cost per completed hire, then build a first-year employment budget. Include internal time consistently without double-counting onboarding.
metaDescription: Calculate recruiting cost per completed hire, then build a first-year employment budget. Include internal time consistently without double-counting onboarding.
opening: Cost per hire divides the recruiting costs included in a defined period by completed hires in that period. Employee cost measures the ongoing cost of employing someone. The two budgets answer different questions and should not be added without checking shared items.
alt: HR manager reviewing interview folders, recruiting invoices and a hiring calendar in a professional small-business office.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
Cost per hire divides the recruiting costs included in a defined period by completed hires in that period. Employee cost measures the ongoing cost of employing someone. The two budgets answer different questions and should not be added without checking shared items.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Define the recruiting numerator and the hires denominator

Cost per hire = (included external recruiting costs + included internal recruiting costs) ÷ completed hires. External costs may include job ads, agency fees and screening. Internal costs may include recruiting staff and documented interviewer time. Use one written cost policy so months and roles can be compared.

Count actual hires using a consistent event, such as accepted offers or starts, and disclose which event you use. An open vacancy is not a hire. When a period has costs but zero hires, the ratio is undefined; report the spend and zero denominator rather than returning $0 cost per hire. Multi-month campaigns need a reconciliation so costs and outcomes are not silently moved between periods.

Calculate a completed two-hire campaign

Original fictional recruiting period
ItemCalculationCost
Job advertisingCampaign invoices$1,200
Agency/screeningSeparate invoice records$1,800
Recruiter effort30 hours × $40$1,200
Manager interviews20 hours × $60$1,200
Total recruiting costExternal $3,000 + internal $2,400$5,400
Completed hiresTwo starts2
Cost per hire$5,400 ÷ 2$2,700

The hourly values are planning assumptions, not current pay benchmarks. If interviewer salary is already in the internal recruiting pool, do not add the same hours again. A cash-only view might show $3,000 external spend, but it omits $2,400 of valued staff effort; label the two views rather than comparing them as identical metrics.

Build the employment budget separately

For one illustrative role, assume $48,000 salary, $4,800 employer charges, $3,600 benefits, $1,200 equipment/software and $1,000 onboarding paid time outside the recruiting definition. The first-year employment budget before recruitment is $58,600. Adding the separately assigned $2,700 recruitment cost gives $61,300.

These are chosen amounts, not a payroll tax or benefit rate. A hiring bonus, relocation payment, training time or recruiter salary must appear only once under the adopted boundary. Recurring-year cost can differ from first-year cost because recruiting and equipment are not necessarily repeated.

Distinguish hiring efficiency from hiring quality

A lower cost per hire does not prove a better hire. Compare like roles and channels, then review acceptance, start dates, retention and observed job performance. A cheap process with repeated replacement hires can cost more overall. Small samples also move sharply: one additional start changes a two-hire denominator by 50%.

Time to fill, recruiting conversion yield and cost per productive hour answer other questions. A team may hire quickly but lack work, onboarding capacity or cash to support the position. Use the employee cost calculator for recurring and productive-hour economics, and the dated cash forecast for the payroll funding period.

Keep a recruiting ledger that can be reproduced

  1. Choose the reporting period and the counted hire event.
  2. List invoices and internal hours with an owner and source reference.
  3. Document shared-cost allocation and any excluded costs.
  4. Reconcile hires, costs, open campaigns and timing differences.
  5. Compare channels only after matching cost and role definitions.

Keep applicant records secure and use job-related review criteria. The financial worksheet does not determine employment-law obligations, eligibility or candidate suitability.

faq.q: Does cost per hire include annual salary?
faq.a: The employee’s ongoing annual salary belongs in the employment budget, not automatically in recruiting cost. Recruiting staff effort can be part of internal recruiting costs.

faq.q: What if no one was hired?
faq.a: Report recruiting spend and zero completed hires. Division by zero does not produce a meaningful cost-per-hire result.

faq.q: How should internal interview time be valued?
faq.a: Use a documented, consistently applied hourly cost or internal rate. Keep it separate from cash-only recruiting spend and avoid adding the same staff cost twice.

faq.q: Is lower cost per hire always better?
faq.a: No. Role mix, timing, sample size, retention and hiring outcomes affect the comparison. A low ratio can conceal repeated replacement hiring.

title: Financial Contingency Plan: Cash Triggers, Actions and Funding
seoTitle: Financial Contingency Plan & Template
description: Build a financial contingency plan with dated cash scenarios, triggers, owners and verified funding. Test an original cash-gap example and response worksheet.
metaDescription: Build a financial contingency plan with dated cash scenarios, triggers, owners and verified funding. Test an original cash-gap example and response worksheet.
opening: A financial contingency plan defines what the business will do when cash assumptions fail: the trigger, decision owner, dated response and funding actually available. It complements the cash forecast and operational continuity plan; it is not a promise that emergency finance will be approved.
alt: Business owner examining a cash-payment calendar, downside scenario and confirmed backup funding folder.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
A financial contingency plan defines what the business will do when cash assumptions fail: the trigger, decision owner, dated response and funding actually available. It complements the cash forecast and operational continuity plan; it is not a promise that emergency finance will be approved.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Connect a risk to a date and an accountable action

Choose a planning horizon that captures your payment commitments. List opening usable cash, expected receipts and committed payments by week or date. Separate restricted balances, unapproved borrowing and expected insurance recoveries from cash available to pay bills. Identify which receipts depend on customer acceptance, processing delays or unresolved disputes.

For each risk, record the event, a measurable trigger, the owner, the response deadline, the action’s cash effect and the dependency that could prevent it. A reserve target should follow the business’s downside timing and tolerance, not an unexplained percentage copied from another company.

Model the shortage before assuming a funding solution

Original fictional four-week cash case, before corrective action
CaseOpening usable cashReceiptsPaymentsClosing cash
Base$18,000$8,000$20,000$6,000
Customer delay$18,000$2,000$20,000$0
Delay plus repair$18,000$2,000$22,500−$2,500

Use a chosen $5,000 minimum cash floor for this case. The base case stays $1,000 above it. The customer-delay case needs $5,000 of timely improvement to restore the floor, and the combined downside needs $7,500. These are aggregate four-week checks; a payroll payment before the week-four receipt may create an earlier, larger need. The dated worksheet must test that ordering.

Build a response that can actually occur before the bill

Illustrative response to the combined downside
ActionCash improvementEvidence needed
Move discretionary equipment purchase$2,000Purchase not committed; no penalty
Reschedule a supplier payment by agreement$1,500Written acceptance and new due date
Available credit draw$4,000Existing facility, conditions met, timely draw
Total improvement$7,500Do not count unconfirmed actions
Revised closing cash$5,000−$2,500 + $7,500

Deferring a payment shifts the obligation into a later period; it does not eliminate the cost. Add the new payment date and debt service to later weeks. Avoid showing credit as ordinary revenue. If the lender can suspend the line or the business fails its conditions, the draw must not appear as dependable cash.

Write an escalation ladder with a decision owner

An illustrative green level is forecast cash at or above the chosen floor, with a weekly review. Amber begins when a dated forecast falls below that floor or a material receipt slips: the finance owner confirms collection status and pauses uncommitted discretionary spending. Red is an inability to meet a critical due payment: the owner escalates immediately, verifies financing and contacts the affected counterparties before making unsupported promises.

The numbers and color levels belong to this fictional case. In a real plan, set them around payroll, critical suppliers, legal commitments, funding terms and operational resilience. Do not advise missing tax or wage obligations as a routine liquidity tactic.

Rehearse the plan and reconcile it after each review

Test a delayed receipt, a lost customer, an equipment failure and a funding source that is unavailable at the same time. Keep source evidence for cash, counterparties, approvals and facility conditions. Check after the event whether the action occurred on time and whether a temporary fix created another shortage.

Use the 13-week cash forecast for dated payments, the cash-flow recovery guide for causes and responses, and your business plan for the assumptions and owners. title: Accounts Receivable vs Accounts Payable: One Invoice, Two Ledgers
seoTitle: Receivables vs Payables: Entries & Cash
description: Compare receivables and payables with matched entries. Reconcile an invoice, credit and partial payment without confusing revenue, expense and cash.
metaDescription: Compare receivables and payables with matched entries. Reconcile an invoice, credit and partial payment without confusing revenue, expense and cash.
opening: Accounts receivable is an amount customers owe your business; accounts payable is an amount your business owes suppliers. The same credit transaction can create the seller’s receivable and the buyer’s payable, but each business keeps its own ledger and payment dates.
alt: Customer invoice folder and supplier bill folder on opposite sides of an oak desk with a payment calendar between them.

html:
Accounts receivable is an amount customers owe your business; accounts payable is an amount your business owes suppliers. The same credit transaction can create the seller’s receivable and the buyer’s payable, but each business keeps its own ledger and payment dates.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Compare the direction, classification and supporting records

Ordinary trade-account comparison; the accounting framework still applies
QuestionAccounts receivableAccounts payable
Who owes whom?Customer owes the businessBusiness owes supplier
Usual balance-sheet categoryAssetLiability
Main evidenceSales invoice, credit, receiptSupplier bill, credit, payment
Normal increase entryDebit ARCredit AP
Cash event when settledBusiness receives cashBusiness pays cash

Trade balances are often current, but classification depends on the operating cycle and terms. A debit or credit is an accounting direction, not a synonym for good or bad. Customer deposits and prepayments can require other accounts; do not force every balance into ordinary AR or AP.

Follow an invoice, credit and partial payment

In a fictional accrual-basis example with no tax, Harbor Supplies delivers $3,000 of materials to a customer on November 5, with payment due December 5. The customer receives and records the materials as inventory. On November 12, a valid $300 return is accepted. On November 25, the customer pays $1,000. The remaining open balance is $1,700.

Matched entries; seller inventory/COGS entries are outside this comparison
EventSeller ledgerBuyer ledger
Invoice / deliveryDebit AR $3,000; credit revenue $3,000Debit inventory $3,000; credit AP $3,000
Accepted returnDebit sales returns $300; credit AR $300Debit AP $300; credit inventory $300
Partial paymentDebit cash $1,000; credit AR $1,000Debit AP $1,000; credit cash $1,000
Open amount$3,000 − $300 − $1,000 = $1,700$3,000 − $300 − $1,000 = $1,700

The seller’s inventory cost and related cost-of-sales reversal are excluded from this narrowly matched ledger example because the acquisition cost was not given. A complete accounting record must include them where applicable. Sales tax, foreign currency, discounts, impairment and framework-specific recognition require additional treatment.

The payment changes cash without creating the same revenue twice

The seller’s invoiced net sales in this case are $2,700 after the return, but the cash collected so far is $1,000. The receipt reduces AR; it is not another $1,000 of accrual revenue. The buyer’s payment reduces AP; it does not automatically create another expense. Buying inventory is also different from recognizing cost of goods sold when that inventory is sold.

The outstanding $1,700 affects collection or payment planning. Put its expected settlement date into the cash forecast. The balance alone does not say whether it is overdue; compare it with the agreed due date and any dispute or amendment.

Reconcile the open balances instead of relying only on totals

For AR, opening balance plus invoices less credits, receipts and applicable write-offs should explain the closing ledger. For AP, opening balance plus accepted bills less credits and payments should explain the closing ledger. Reconcile customer/supplier subledgers with the control account, then match settlement amounts to the bank.

Review unapplied receipts, duplicate bills, unmatched credits and cut-off errors. Keep disputed amounts visible. Amounts due from and to the same counterparty should not be netted casually: applicable offsetting rules and agreements matter. Use aging buckets based on a consistently stated method, such as days past due.

Choose the detailed workflow after understanding the difference

AR management concerns invoicing, collection, disputes and customer credit exposure. AP management concerns approved bills, valid suppliers, due dates and controlled disbursement. This comparison does not replace either full process. For the collection-speed calculation, use DSO; for the broader balance relationship, use working capital. Keep the historical cash-flow statement separate from the forecast of future dates.

title: Cost Performance Index: Earned Value, Actual Cost and Forecast Limits
seoTitle: Cost Performance Index: CPI Formula
description: Calculate CPI from earned value and actual cost. Check weighted totals, separate project cost performance from margin and compare remaining-work forecasts.
metaDescription: Calculate CPI from earned value and actual cost. Check weighted totals, separate project cost performance from margin and compare remaining-work forecasts.
opening: Cost Performance Index, or CPI, equals earned value divided by actual cost for the same project scope and status date. It measures the budgeted value of completed work per dollar of actual cost; it does not measure sales revenue or profit margin.
alt: Project manager comparing approved completed milestones with an actual-cost ledger beside workshop plans.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
Cost Performance Index, or CPI, equals earned value divided by actual cost for the same project scope and status date. It measures the budgeted value of completed work per dollar of actual cost; it does not measure sales revenue or profit margin.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

Define planned value, earned value and actual cost

Planned value is the approved budget for work scheduled by the status date. Earned value is the approved budget for work actually completed by that date, using a defensible completion method. Actual cost records what that completed work has cost on a consistent accounting basis. Match scope, cut-off and currency before dividing.

CPI = EV ÷ AC. Below 1 means the measured work has consumed more actual cost than its budgeted value; above 1 means the opposite. A zero actual-cost denominator needs investigation, not a fabricated finite index. Missing supplier accruals can make CPI look artificially favorable.

Calculate cost and schedule performance separately

Original fictional project status date
MeasureAmount / resultMeaning
Budget at completion (BAC)$100,000Approved project budget
Planned value (PV)$60,000Budgeted work scheduled so far
Earned value (EV)$50,000Budgeted completed work
Actual cost (AC)$62,500Cost recognized to the status date
CPI0.80$50,000 ÷ $62,500
Cost variance−$12,500EV − AC
Schedule performance index0.8333EV ÷ PV

The project has earned $0.80 of budgeted work for each actual dollar. CPI does not mean a 20% profit loss, and the schedule index does not directly convert into days late. In this example, cost performance and scheduled completion both require investigation, but they describe different dimensions.

Choose an estimate-at-completion assumption explicitly

If all remaining work can be delivered at its original remaining budget, EAC is AC + (BAC − EV): $62,500 + $50,000 = $112,500. If the same cost efficiency is assumed to continue across the total project, EAC is BAC ÷ CPI: $100,000 ÷ 0.80 = $125,000. The $12,500 gap is an assumption difference, not an arithmetic error.

A bottom-up remaining estimate of $58,000 would instead produce EAC of $120,500. Document supplier commitments, remaining quantities, rework and resource rates behind that estimate. Do not select the most reassuring formula without checking what is causing the variance. EAC is a forecast, not a confirmed final invoice.

Aggregate dollars before calculating portfolio CPI

Suppose work package A has EV $30,000 and AC $25,000, so CPI is 1.2. Package B has EV $20,000 and AC $37,500, so CPI is approximately 0.5333. The simple average of the two indices is 0.8667, but project CPI is ($30,000 + $20,000) ÷ ($25,000 + $37,500) = 0.80. Weighting follows the underlying totals.

Verify completion evidence rather than treating dollars spent as percentage complete. An expensive early purchase can increase actual cost while little eligible work is earned; a milestone-based rule can delay earned value. State those rules and apply them consistently.

Turn the ratio into a corrective project decision

  1. Confirm baseline, completion evidence and status-date cut-off.
  2. Investigate quantity, rate, productivity, scope and rework causes.
  3. Re-estimate the remaining work from supported inputs.
  4. Choose and fund the response; log approved scope changes.
  5. Review the next status date without erasing the original baseline history.

Use job-order costing for recorded job cost and budget variance analysis for driver-specific performance. CPI is a project earned-value measure, separate from a business operating margin.

faq.a: No. Earned value is budgeted completed work, not customer revenue. A CPI of 0.8 is not an 80% margin.

faq.q: Does EAC equal BAC divided by CPI in every situation?
faq.a: No. That formula assumes the measured cost efficiency continues. A remaining-at-budget or bottom-up estimate uses different assumptions.

faq.q: Can I average work-package CPI values?
faq.a: Calculate total earned value divided by total actual cost. A simple average of ratios can misstate the project because packages have different cost weights.

faq.q: What happens when actual cost is zero?
faq.a: The division is undefined. Investigate missing costs, timing or completion rules rather than presenting a finite CPI value.

title: Profitability Index: Discounted Cash Flows and Project Selection
seoTitle: Profitability Index: Formula & NPV Example
description: Calculate profitability index from discounted cash flows. Reconcile NPV, compare project scale and avoid ranking indivisible investments by a ratio alone.
metaDescription: Calculate profitability index from discounted cash flows. Reconcile NPV, compare project scale and avoid ranking indivisible investments by a ratio alone.
opening: Profitability index compares the present value of a project’s future net cash flows with its positive initial investment. Under the stated conventional setup, PI above 1 corresponds to positive NPV, but the ratio alone does not select the best combination of projects.
alt: Business owner comparing an equipment investment with future dated cash-flow cards and a capital-project folder.
imageCaption: Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional.
html:
Profitability index compares the present value of a project’s future net cash flows with its positive initial investment. Under the stated conventional setup, PI above 1 corresponds to positive NPV, but the ratio alone does not select the best combination of projects.

Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction.

State the cash-flow convention before calculating PI

PI = present value of future net project cash flows ÷ initial investment. Here the investment occurs at time zero, future amounts are net incremental project cash flows, and discounting uses end-of-year timing. NPV = present value of future net cash flows − initial investment. With these conventions and a positive initial outlay, PI = 1 + NPV ÷ initial investment.

Some sources use a different numerator or treat later investment outlays separately. Do not compare such ratios without reconciling the definitions. A zero initial investment makes this version undefined. Nonconventional cash flows and multiple later capital commitments need an explicitly rebuilt model.

Discount the same project year by year

Original fictional project; 10% illustrative discount rate
TimeNet project cash flowDiscount calculationPresent value
0−$20,000Initial investment−$20,000.00
Year 1$9,0009000 ÷ 1.10$8,181.82
Year 2$9,0009000 ÷ 1.10²$7,438.02
Year 3$9,0009000 ÷ 1.10³$6,761.83
Future PV total$27,000 nominalSum of unrounded PV$22,381.67

PI is $22,381.6679 ÷ $20,000 = 1.1191. NPV is $2,381.67. Retain unrounded discount factors until the final display. The 10% rate is an illustrative input, not a recommended return, borrowing quote or risk-adjusted rate for your business.

A ratio above one is not an annual return

A PI of 1.1191 means about $1.1191 of discounted future net cash flows for each $1 initially invested in this defined case. It is not an 11.91% annual ROI. Project timing, risk, taxes, replacement needs and a suitable discount rate affect the interpretation. Accounting profit and EBITDA are not substitutes for incremental project cash flow.

At the same 10% discount rate, reducing each future annual cash flow to $8,000 gives future PV of about $19,894.82, PI of 0.9947 and NPV of −$105.18. A modest assumption change crosses the acceptability threshold, so retain a sensitivity table rather than only the base-case label.

Use NPV and constraints when comparing alternatives

Consider project A requiring $10,000 with future PV $13,000: PI is 1.30 and NPV $3,000. Project B requires $30,000 with future PV $36,000: PI is 1.20 and NPV $6,000. If the projects are mutually exclusive and risk, timing and other constraints are comparable, choosing the higher ratio alone would miss B’s larger dollar NPV.

Under a fixed budget with indivisible projects, evaluate feasible combinations. Dividing a project into fractions is not automatically possible. Include dependencies, available funding, staff capacity, required assets and strategic obligations. A ratio ranking can assist analysis; it is not a universal capital-allocation rule.

Build a defensible project cash schedule

  1. Specify the decision and the alternative being compared.
  2. List incremental cash inflows, operating outflows, working-capital changes, later investment and terminal recoveries.
  3. Use consistent timing, currency, nominal/real treatment and tax assumptions.
  4. Document the chosen discount rate and review sensitivities.
  5. Reconcile PI to NPV and confirm feasibility before approval.

faq.a: No. It expresses discounted value relative to initial outlay under the selected horizon and rate, not a compound annual return.

title: Landscaping Working Capital: Fund the Seasonal Cash Gap
seoTitle: Landscaping Working Capital: Seasonal Cash Gap
description: Build a dated landscaping cash schedule for materials, payroll and customer receipts. Test the funding gap, minimum cash floor and delayed-payment scenario.
metaDescription: Build a dated landscaping cash schedule for materials, payroll and customer receipts. Test the funding gap, minimum cash floor and delayed-payment scenario.
scopeBoundary: Seasonal dated operating funding; general working-capital definitions and landscaping break-even remain existing owners.
opening: Landscaping working-capital needs depend on when materials, crew payroll and overhead must be paid compared with when customer cash clears. Build a dated cash schedule, find its lowest balance and test a delayed-receipt case before choosing a funding amount.
alt: Landscaping owner reviewing supplier slips and a payroll calendar beside spring nursery materials.
html:
Landscaping working-capital needs depend on when materials, crew payroll and overhead must be paid compared with when customer cash clears. Build a dated cash schedule, find its lowest balance and test a delayed-receipt case before choosing a funding amount.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Separate the balance-sheet measure from the seasonal funding gap

Net working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. That balance-sheet measure is useful, but it does not say whether Friday’s payroll clears before Monday’s customer payment. A profitable landscaping job can require temporary funding if plants, soil, fuel and labor are paid first.

Start the cash schedule with reconciled, available business cash. List each receipt by its expected clearing date and each payment by its actual due date. Include equipment purchases, debt payments and owner withdrawals in separate lines when relevant. Those lines affect funding even though they do not all belong in operating profit. Do not count an unapproved credit limit or a customer promise as cleared cash.

A spring ramp-up with materials paid before collections

Illustrative April 2027 cash schedule; no borrowing in this base case
Week endingOpening cashReceiptsPaymentsClosing cash
April 2$12,000$2,000$10,000$4,000
April 9$4,000$4,000$11,000−$3,000
April 16−$3,000$12,000$8,000$1,000
April 23$1,000$10,000$7,000$4,000

Week one includes $6,000 materials, $3,000 payroll and $1,000 other payments. Week two includes $4,000 materials, $5,000 payroll and $2,000 other payments. Total receipts are $28,000 and total payments $36,000, so $12,000 + $28,000 − $36,000 = $4,000 closing cash. The lowest weekly closing balance is −$3,000. A negative forecast is a funding warning, not an instruction to let a bank account overdraw.

If management chooses a $5,000 minimum cash floor, the additional cash needed at the lowest weekly close is $5,000 − (−$3,000) = $8,000. The floor is a choice for this case, not a landscaping-industry standard. Check daily order within each week: a Monday payroll before a Friday receipt can create a deeper trough.

Delay one receipt without inventing a second payment

Move $6,000 of the April 16 receipts to April 23. Week-three receipts become $6,000 and week-four receipts $16,000. Closing balances become $4,000, −$3,000, −$5,000 and $4,000. The total month’s receipts and closing cash are unchanged, but the low point falls to −$5,000. Keeping the same floor now needs $10,000 additional cash at that weekly close.

Do not add the late receipt to the later week while leaving it in the original week. Reconcile every scheduled invoice to one open receipt record. Record evidence for customer approval, invoice disputes, deposits and clearing delays. A deposit may also carry delivery or refund obligations; it is not automatically earned profit.

Match the response to the timing and the underlying margin

Possible management responses include staging materials by job, agreeing milestone billing before work starts, aligning valid supplier terms with collections or evaluating a documented funding facility. Compare actual fees, repayment dates, availability conditions and the downside forecast. This schedule does not establish eligibility or recommend a lender.

Re-run the later weeks after any payment deferral or borrowing. Moving a supplier bill does not remove it, and a draw creates a repayment obligation. If each job loses money after its relevant costs, short-term funding only delays that problem. Check the seasonal landscaping break-even guide for operating recovery and the working-capital calculation guide for account definitions.

Keep a seasonal review tied to job and bank records

  1. Reconcile cash, open invoices, purchase commitments and payroll dates at the same cutoff.
  2. Update the next 13 weeks by clearing date, with daily detail near the tightest dates.
  3. Separate confirmed work from unaccepted quotes and isolate customer concentration.
  4. Assign an owner and deadline to each proposed funding or collection action.
  5. Archive the forecast, compare cleared results and investigate date or amount differences.

Use the 13-week cash-flow forecast for the dated model and the landscaping business plan for the wider operating assumptions. Extend the horizon through winter commitments instead of stopping the forecast at the first profitable month.

description: Compare six small-business models using customer evidence, startup cash, contribution and owner-hours. Use a practical screening worksheet before investing.

A useful small-business idea fits a specific customer problem, a deliverable offer and the cash and hours you can commit. Screen possible models against real demand and operating constraints before choosing one from a list.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Compare models by what must be true

Six starting points to investigate, not earnings recommendations
ModelCustomer problemMain constraintFirst evidence to collect
Recurring home cleaningReliable scheduled cleaningTravel, crew time and reworkLocal paid trial and repeat booking
Bookkeeping supportTimely organized business recordsCompetence, access and scopeOwner interviews and defined pilot
Product photographyUsable catalog imagesEditing time and revisionsPaid sample with acceptance criteria
Plant-care visitsMaintained office plantsRoute density and replacement costsNearby-site trial and travel log
Made-to-order alterationsClothing fit or repairSkilled production hoursPaid job with measured completion time
Specialty resaleHard-to-find selected productsInventory, returns and cash cycleSmall-batch sell-through and net receipts

These models have different operating burdens. A home service can avoid inventory while still needing transport, insurance and practical schedule capacity. A digital service can avoid a storefront while creating customer-acquisition, software and revision costs. A product business can show sales growth while cash remains tied up in unsold stock.

Use disqualifying constraints before scoring enthusiasm

Write your available cash, weekly hours, required personal income, relevant skills, geographic reach and unacceptable commitments. Exclude ideas that cannot meet those constraints under a plausible downside case. For regulated or sensitive work, verify the actual professional, insurance and local requirements before accepting customers. A broad idea list cannot establish permission to practice.

Then compare demand evidence, contribution per constrained hour, startup commitments, time to collection and repeatability. Keep unknowns visible instead of assigning a precise score to an unsupported guess. A signed paid pilot is stronger evidence than compliments from friends, but a single pilot still does not prove recurring demand.

Compare two fictional pilots on the same cost boundary

Original pilot economics; both cases exclude general overhead and income tax
MeasureCleaning visitPhotography package
Price$180$450
Relevant cash delivery costs$55$90
Contribution before owner time$125$360

The photography package has a larger ticket, but $360 divided by 12 hours is $30 per hour; cleaning yields $125 divided by four, or $31.25. Neither figure is take-home pay. They must still cover the included owner-income requirement, fixed costs, idle time and any omitted commitments. If the cleaning visit needs five hours instead of four, contribution per hour falls to $25.

Suppose a month offers 80 practical owner-hours and 20 hours are needed for prospecting and general administration outside those job totals. The remaining 60 hours support at most 15 four-hour visits or five twelve-hour photography packages. Customer demand might be below either ceiling. Avoid multiplying a full calendar by a price before checking all the hours.

Design a small test with a stop rule

Choose one customer segment and one tightly specified offer. Ask how the customer currently solves the problem, what causes dissatisfaction and how buying decisions are made. Compare actual alternatives and test a paid delivery at the intended price where practical. Record acquisition effort, delivery time, changes, refunds and collection dates.

Before the test, set a spending ceiling and a decision rule. For example: test three paid jobs, keep total test cash below a chosen $400 limit and investigate any job that needs over five hours. Those are fictional experiment settings, not universal validation thresholds. If the test misses the rule, revise scope or stop; do not redefine success after seeing the result.

Turn the best-supported model into a funding plan

Obtain dated supplier quotes and identify one-time, recurring and refundable amounts. Include operating shortfalls before customers pay, a separately chosen reserve and the owner’s own living needs outside the business budget. Avoid adding the same startup payment to both setup spending and the cash-gap total.

The startup cost calculator helps organize cash needs; the business plan template records the chosen model. When you need a demand schedule, use the small-business sales forecast. Choose the idea because the evidence and constraints fit, then preserve the assumptions so the first month’s actual results can challenge them.

After selecting an offer, follow the startup roadmap. For a client engagement, use the proposal and delivery-cost record before committing to scope.

Start a small business by confirming a customer problem, testing a specific offer, estimating delivery economics and dated cash needs, then completing the requirements for your location and opening with reliable records. Review actual results before increasing commitments.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Define the first customer and the smallest useful offer

Describe who buys, the outcome they want, the alternative they use and the scope you can deliver consistently. Interview likely buyers and compare local alternatives. A large market estimate is not a list of customers who will buy from you. Keep confirmed orders, customer interest and assumptions in separate categories.

Test price and scope together. Record the time and cash required to deliver a paid pilot, including revisions, travel, payment fees and customer support. Choose a spending ceiling and a date to decide whether to continue. Use the business-idea screening guide when you are still choosing between models.

Reconcile setup spending and early operating cash

Fictional launch plan for a small service business
Cash requirementAmountBoundary
Tools and setup purchases$2,400Paid before opening
Security deposit$600Cash paid; not assumed expense
First two months operating shortfall$2,000Receipts less payments after setup
Chosen cash cushion$1,500Separate management assumption
Total initial funding need$6,500No setup amounts counted twice
Owner cash committed$4,500Confirmed available source
Unfunded difference$2,000Resolve before commitments

The funding need is $2,400 + $600 + $2,000 + $1,500 = $6,500. Subtracting $4,500 confirmed owner cash leaves $2,000 unresolved. That difference is not automatically an approved loan. Reduce or stage commitments, obtain documented funding or postpone launch until the dated schedule works. Include any financing fees, interest and repayments when a specific option is assessed.

The $2,000 shortfall means operating cash outflows exceed receipts by that amount during the two-month schedule, after excluding the separately listed setup payments. If your forecast already contains those setup payments, do not add them a second time. Budget household living costs separately and confirm what the owner must withdraw from the business.

Check whether the offer can cover the monthly requirement

Suppose one service sells for $250 and its defined job-linked costs are $100. Contribution is $150 per completed job. Covering $1,200 monthly business overhead requires eight jobs before owner compensation, interest and tax under that cost boundary. Adding a separately chosen $2,400 owner-income planning requirement raises the combined target to 24 jobs: ($1,200 + $2,400) ÷ $150.

If delivery takes four hours per job, 24 jobs require 96 job-hours, plus selling and administration outside the quoted job time. Check your practical calendar and expected demand. A personal income target is not necessarily a deductible accounting expense; label it as a planning requirement. The startup calculator helps organize launch assumptions without replacing that distinction.

Complete the requirements for the actual business

Use the SBA’s launch guidance as a starting point to identify questions about structure, name registration, tax identifiers, banking, permits and insurance. Requirements depend on activity, state and locality. Verify current obligations with the relevant government agencies and advisers before trading; there is no single checklist that grants permission for every US business.

Keep business transactions identifiable from the start. Establish invoice numbering, supplier records, receipt storage, expense categories and bank reconciliation. Confirm who maintains the books and how payroll or customer deposits will be handled if relevant. Do not choose a structure solely from a generic cost comparison without considering the actual ownership and obligations.

Launch with a short review cycle and a visible cash cutoff

  1. Confirm the offer, price, delivery scope and customer acceptance process.
  2. Resolve the funding schedule and distinguish committed funds from applications.
  3. Check required registrations and operational permissions for the real location.
  4. Record the first invoices, receipts, delivery costs and work hours.
  5. Compare the first month with the original assumptions and approve the next commitments.

Use the business plan template to connect the evidence and funding decision. Use the 13-week cash forecast for payment dates and rolling forecasting for future operating assumptions. Preserve the original forecast so later changes remain explainable.

A Business Model Canvas summarizes how one business model serves customers and earns revenue through nine connected blocks. Its value comes from testing the relationships between those blocks, including whether the proposed price, costs and delivery capacity can work together.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Fill the nine blocks for one model

Original fictional example: recurring small-office cleaning
BlockIllustrative hypothesisEvidence needed
Customer segmentsNearby offices needing after-hours cleaningBuyer interviews and site criteria
Value propositionsConsistent scoped service with documented completionPilot and customer acceptance
ChannelsLocal referrals and direct outreachCost and conversion records
Customer relationshipsNamed contact and monthly scope reviewRetention and issue records
Revenue streamsMonthly contracted service feeAccepted terms and collections
Key resourcesTrained crew, transport and equipmentAvailable hours and quotes
Key activitiesScheduling, cleaning, checks and invoicingTime log and quality checks
Key partnersSupply vendor and backup supportActual availability and terms
Cost structureJob-linked labor/supplies plus period overheadCost ledger and commitments

The framework is associated with Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur and Strategyzer. Use the official Strategyzer canvas for the original tool and its applicable usage terms. The table and worksheet here are an independently written case and evidence record, not an official Strategyzer template.

Connect the customer promise to the operating numbers

Assume ten office customers each pay $600 a month: revenue is $6,000. Each requires eight worker-hours at a defined loaded delivery cost of $30 per hour, so delivery labor is $2,400. Supplies are $30 per customer, or $300. Contribution after those included delivery costs is $3,300. Subtract $1,800 defined monthly overhead for an illustrative $1,500 operating result before omitted financing and tax items.

Ten customers need 80 worker-hours. If practical delivery capacity is 96 hours, the same eight-hour scope supports at most 12 whole customers, before considering route and scheduling constraints. A promise of unlimited additional service contradicts the cost and capacity blocks. Do not count the same salaried labor in both the $30 hourly rate and the $1,800 overhead.

Change a block and follow the consequences

Suppose the value proposition changes to include two extra worker-hours per customer at the same fee. Ten customers now require 100 hours, exceeding the stated 96-hour capacity. At the same $30 cost rate, delivery labor becomes $3,000, contribution $2,700 and the result after unchanged overhead $900. That arithmetic does not make the schedule feasible: an actual capacity response may add further cost.

The choice could require a narrower scope, a justified price change, a different customer segment or additional resources. Update channels and relationship expectations as well as the spreadsheet. A model canvas should expose those dependencies rather than hide them behind separate attractive statements.

Rank assumptions by consequence and missing evidence

Mark every statement as observed, supported by a limited test or still assumed. Customer willingness to pay, delivery time and repeat purchase deserve early attention because they can change several blocks at once. Write a test with a customer group, offer, cost ceiling, measured outcome and decision date.

For the cleaning case, time a fully scoped pilot including travel and inspection, then obtain a separate repeat-service decision. An enthusiastic survey response is not equivalent to paid recurring demand. Archive the original canvas and change only the blocks the evidence affects; record why each version differs.

Use the right next document for the decision

A canvas describes the model; a feasibility study examines whether it should proceed under actual constraints. A business plan organizes the chosen venture’s operating and funding story. A sales forecast translates demand assumptions into a dated volume schedule. None of those documents independently proves a profitable business.

Continue with the business plan template, the customer profitability method for cost-to-serve differences or the sales forecast for demand and capacity. Keep the canvas focused on one coherent model so its assumptions can be challenged together.

The feasibility study tests whether the model can proceed; strategic planning records which customers and resource priorities the business will choose.

A business proposal explains a specific client problem, the deliverables you will provide, the schedule, price, assumptions and process for acceptance. Build the delivery cost case before promising the scope, then turn the agreed details into the appropriate written engagement.

Use a proposal the client can evaluate

Editable proposal sections and the question each answers
SectionWhat to writeReview control
Client objectiveSpecific problem and agreed success evidenceConfirm the buyer recognizes it
DeliverablesNamed outputs, quantities and formatsDefine completion for each output
Scope and exclusionsIncluded work and explicit boundariesAvoid unlimited revisions
ScheduleMilestones and client inputsIdentify dependencies and decision dates
PriceFee, assumptions and applicable tax treatmentReconcile included and optional amounts
PaymentAmounts, milestones and due-date basisMatch contract and invoice terms
AcceptanceAuthorized parties, scope approval and dateObtain suitable engagement review

A proposal can answer a request for proposals or start a conversation with a potential buyer. In either case, adapt it to the decision the client must make. A business plan explains the venture to owners or funders; a client proposal offers a defined engagement. Do not substitute a generic company history for an answer to the client’s requirement.

Check a fictional fixed-fee project before quoting

A catalog photography proposal includes 20 finished images, one agreed background treatment and one consolidated correction round within the stated scope. The seller estimates 20 production hours plus ten planning, communication and editing hours. At an internal loaded rate of $40, included labor is $1,200. Add $300 studio and materials and $150 travel for a defined delivery cost of $1,650.

At a $2,400 fee, contribution after those included costs is $750, or 31.25% of the fee. Markup on that same $1,650 cost is 45.45%. The percentages use different denominators. Neither establishes net company profit because shared overhead and other omitted costs still need coverage. The $40 rate must represent the chosen cost basis consistently.

Show how one scope change affects the quote

Ten extra hours at the same internal rate add $400. If the fee stays $2,400, included delivery cost becomes $2,050 and contribution falls to $350, or 14.58%. If the client also needs new props, travel or a new deadline, the cost change may be larger. An undefined revision promise makes the original estimate unreliable.

State which customer inputs are required, how feedback is consolidated, what counts as an accepted output and how requested changes are evaluated. Record the proposed impact on scope, delivery dates and fee before commencing additional work. This teaching template does not establish enforceable contract terms for every jurisdiction.

Connect milestones to actual cash requirements

An illustrative 40% / 40% / 20% payment schedule splits the $2,400 fee into $960, $960 and $480. The schedule must be negotiated, documented and matched to the work and invoice dates. A milestone described in a proposal is not a cleared payment. Test the cash schedule if the second installment arrives late.

Do not promise the client an unsupported revenue increase to justify the price. Use measurable deliverable acceptance or explicitly labeled scenarios instead. Taxes, intellectual property, confidentiality, cancellation and liability depend on the actual engagement; resolve those terms with suitable review rather than treating this example as a complete legal agreement.

Complete and review the proposal before sending

  1. Replace the sample client, objective, deliverables and assumptions.
  2. Recompute all hours, costs, optional items and the total fee.
  3. Check the planned completion date against practical capacity and client dependencies.
  4. Reconcile milestone amounts to the total and record the due-date basis.
  5. Review commercial and legal terms for the actual engagement and retain the accepted version.

Use the downloadable worksheet as an editable proposal record, including blank acceptance fields. The customer profitability guide helps evaluate account support beyond the initial job, while the contribution-margin method checks the chosen delivery-cost boundary. Use the cash forecast to test payment timing.

When demand for the engagement grows, compare growth options against delivery capacity before promising a wider scope.

title: Business Growth Strategies: Compare Contribution, Capacity and Cash

description: Compare retention, pricing, added volume and channel growth with original financial cases. Test contribution, bottlenecks and funding before committing.

scopeBoundary: Overview of growth choices; specific location/expansion investment remains a separate owner.
opening: A business growth strategy should explain which customers and offers will generate more useful contribution, what capacity is required and how the change will be funded before cash arrives. Higher sales alone do not establish a better or affordable business.

html:
A business growth strategy should explain which customers and offers will generate more useful contribution, what capacity is required and how the change will be funded before cash arrives. Higher sales alone do not establish a better or affordable business.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Choose a growth mechanism before choosing a spending budget

Growth choices to test against actual evidence
OptionEvidence neededCost or constraint to test
Retain existing customersRepeat purchase and churn recordsSupport effort and retention incentives
Improve price or scopeBuyer acceptance and offer comparisonLost volume and delivery changes
Sell more through the current channelConversion and demand recordsAcquisition cost and practical capacity
Add a channel or segmentPilot with separately tracked economicsFees, returns and collections
Add an offer for existing buyersProblem and willingness-to-pay evidenceDevelopment, training and complexity
Increase delivery capacityVerified backlog and bottleneckFixed commitments and ramp-up cash

Compare options using the same period and cost boundary. A discount may increase orders while lowering total contribution. A new channel may bring demand but add commissions or slower settlement. Retention can reduce replacement selling effort, but it still needs a defined offer and service budget. Test the actual mechanism rather than applying a generic growth percentage.

Compare price, volume and capacity in one fictional business

Independent monthly cases; baseline price 200, job cost 100, overhead 6000
CaseJobs / priceRevenueContributionOverheadResult
Baseline100 / $200$20,000$10,000$6,000$4,000
Price +5%, same volume100 / $210$21,000$11,000$6,000$5,000
Volume +20%, same costs120 / $200$24,000$12,000$6,000$6,000
Volume +20%, new capacity cost120 / $200$24,000$12,000$8,500$3,500

Each job takes two worker-hours. Baseline work requires 200 hours; 120 jobs require 240. If practical capacity is 220, the simple volume case is infeasible without a resource or scope change. The last case assumes a specific $2,500 added monthly commitment and adequate capacity, showing a result below baseline despite higher sales. The price case assumes no volume loss solely to isolate the price effect; customer acceptance still needs evidence.

Fund the ramp before treating the result as available cash

Suppose the extra 20 jobs require $2,000 additional delivery payments before customer cash clears. A $1,000 campaign payment and $2,500 capacity payment are also due before those receipts. The incremental pre-collection cash requirement is $5,500, before fees, timing differences or a chosen reserve. This is a cash schedule, not another $5,500 expense to subtract from the monthly result: some costs are already in the case.

Map every incremental receipt and payment to a date. Distinguish a one-time setup purchase from a recurring capacity commitment. Test customer payment delays and the period after a promotion ends. Review the financial contingency plan for triggers if the growth assumptions fail.

Set limits and compare a pilot with its original case

Choose one offer, channel or segment for the first test. Record incremental acquisition spending, accepted price, realized delivery hours, refund or rework costs and collection dates. Keep comparable existing activity visible: a new channel can shift customers from an existing channel rather than create entirely new demand.

Set an exposure ceiling, review date and response to missed assumptions before launching the test. For example, investigate if delivery rises above the planned two hours or if additional sales require capacity earlier than expected. Those are case-specific controls. Do not claim a pilot caused all extra sales without a defensible comparison.

Decide using profit, bottlenecks and cash together

Approve a next step only when the demand evidence, defined contribution, operational plan and dated cash schedule reconcile. List commitments that cannot be reversed quickly and verify funding conditions. A positive forecast under an unapproved staffing plan is still an unresolved decision.

Use CVP scenarios for cost ranges, the sales forecast for demand and capacity, and ROAS versus ROI when evaluating a paid campaign. Link growth choices to an archived operating forecast so the next review can explain what actually changed.

Translate an approved growth choice into measurable business goals, and record the resource trade-off in the strategic plan.

title: Business Feasibility Study: Should This Venture Proceed?

description: Assess demand, delivery capacity, economics and funding with a worked feasibility study. Use explicit proceed, revise or stop conditions and an editable record.

opening: A business feasibility study investigates whether a defined venture can work under real market, operating, financial and funding constraints. Its output is an evidenced proceed, revise or stop decision with conditions, rather than a document written to justify a decision already made.
