html:
A business feasibility study investigates whether a defined venture can work under real market, operating, financial and funding constraints. Its output is an evidenced proceed, revise or stop decision with conditions, rather than a document written to justify a decision already made.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Define the decision and the alternatives

Specify the offer, customer, delivery model, location where relevant, decision horizon and commitments under consideration. Include a smaller pilot or postponement as real alternatives. A study of “starting a business” is too broad to test supplier quotes, customer acceptance or the cash required before launch.

Decide in advance which evidence would change the answer. Separate confirmed facts from estimates and unknowns. Name the owner, date and source for important assumptions. Feasibility investigates whether the venture should proceed; the subsequent business plan develops how an accepted option will operate.

Test five connected forms of feasibility

Decision questions and evidence
AreaCore questionUseful evidence
MarketWill the defined customer buy at this scope and price?Paid pilot, buyer interviews and alternatives
Technical / operationalCan the team deliver the required quality and volume?Timed process, supplier quotes and capacity
Organizational / requirementsCan the actual team operate within relevant obligations?Competence, permissions and adviser checks
EconomicDoes defined contribution cover the requirement?Reconciled costs, price and scenarios
Funding / timingCan commitments be paid when due?Dated cash schedule and verified funding

Passing one area does not pass the others. A popular product can fail a practical delivery test; a positive accounting result can still require more startup cash than is available. Obtain current specialist input for material location or activity requirements instead of copying a general statement that permits are “easy.”

Work through a constrained service venture

Consider a fictional monthly service priced at $300 with $120 relevant delivery cost per job. Contribution is $180. Period overhead is $5,400, so operating break-even is 30 whole jobs. A separately chosen $3,600 owner-income planning requirement raises the combined recovery target to 50 jobs: ($5,400 + $3,600) ÷ $180.

Each job takes three delivery hours. At 120 practical delivery hours a month, the business can complete only 40 jobs before other constraints. At 40 jobs, revenue is $12,000, delivery costs $4,800 and contribution $7,200. After $5,400 overhead, the result is $1,800, below the chosen owner-income requirement. Calling the idea feasible because it passes 30-job operating break-even would conceal that unmet requirement.

Compare explicit revisions instead of forcing a yes

One option is a $330 price with unchanged $120 job cost. Contribution becomes $210, and the combined $9,000 requirement needs 43 whole jobs after rounding up, still above 40-job capacity. Another option reduces the scoped delivery time to two hours, if quality and customer acceptance can be maintained. At the original $300 price, capacity becomes 60 jobs and the 50-job recovery target becomes operationally possible, but demand remains unproven.

Test revised scope rather than assuming the same job can be rushed without consequence. If the narrower offer loses customers or adds rework, update both the demand and cost cases. Funding remains a separate test: a $9,000 startup cash need against $7,000 confirmed funds leaves $2,000 unresolved even if the revised operating case works.

Write a conditional decision that can be checked

The original model should not receive unconditional approval: the owner-income requirement exceeds the capacity-supported result and a funding gap remains. A reasonable study output is “revise and test the narrower scope, obtain demand evidence at that scope, and resolve the dated $2,000 funding gap before launch commitments.” Record who must deliver each piece of evidence and by when.

Use the startup cost calculator for launch cash, CVP analysis for the cost range and business plan template after choosing a viable alternative. Archive rejected options as well as the approved one so later reviewers can see the trade-offs.

If a revised model passes the decision conditions, continue with the launch roadmap; use the seasonal funding case for an example of dated operating cash needs.

title: Business Goals: Translate Targets into Drivers and Cash
seoTitle: Business Goals: Targets, Capacity and Cash
description: Turn business goals into measurable drivers, ownership and review dates. Reconcile a service growth target with delivery hours, contribution and cash needs.

opening: A useful business goal names an outcome, its baseline, a measure, an owner and a review date. Translate the target into customer activity, delivery capacity and cash requirements before treating it as an achievable commitment.

html:
A useful business goal names an outcome, its baseline, a measure, an owner and a review date. Translate the target into customer activity, delivery capacity and cash requirements before treating it as an achievable commitment.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Separate a goal, a forecast and an action

A goal is an intended result. A forecast is the current evidence-based expectation. An action is something the team will do to influence the result. “Reach $24,000 monthly revenue” is a goal; “current customer evidence supports $21,000” is a forecast; “test one referral offer by the end of the month” is an action. Keep those statements separate so an ambitious goal does not become an unsupported forecast.

The SMART framework helps make objectives specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. It does not independently verify demand, resource availability or cause and effect. Write the baseline and source beside the target, including the reporting period and cost or revenue boundary.

Translate a fictional revenue target into work

A service business currently completes 80 jobs per month at $250: revenue is $20,000. Its goal is $24,000 at the same price within the chosen three-month planning period. That requires 96 jobs, an increase of 16, or 20%. At three worker-hours per job, required delivery time rises from 240 to 288 hours.

Practical available delivery capacity is 270 hours. The target therefore needs 18 additional hours, a valid scope change or a different price/volume mix. A goal can be clear and measurable while still exceeding capacity. Confirm whether the 270 hours already excludes general administration, absence, travel or rework; do not subtract those twice.

Check contribution and the payment cycle

Assume the defined relevant delivery cost is $100 per job. Each job contributes $150 before period overhead and other omitted costs. Sixteen extra jobs add $2,400 contribution if price and cost remain unchanged. That amount is not an approved hiring budget unless the added-capacity plan, overhead effect and owner requirements have been tested.

If those extra jobs require $1,600 delivery payments before customer collections, the growth plan needs a dated cash bridge. A $400 referral test paid in advance increases the illustrative pre-collection outlay to $2,000. Avoid subtracting the $1,600 delivery cost twice from the projected result: it is already included in contribution. Cash timing and profit use the same underlying events in different views.

Give each goal a measure, owner and guardrail

Outcome96 completed jobs per month by review dateAccepted job and completion records
Baseline80 jobs at 250Same period and revenue basis
DriverQualified inquiries, acceptance and repeat workTrack distinct customers and denominators

Cash2000 illustrative pre-collection outlayConfirm dates and available funds

GuardrailNo unapproved scope or quality declineRework, complaints and actual hours

Use a small set of leading measures the team can act on and lagging measures that show the outcome. Calls made alone may rise without useful orders; completed sales alone may hide refunds or unpaid balances. Choose denominators carefully and avoid changing the definition after the target is missed.

Review progress without rewriting the original target

Preserve the approved baseline, goal and forecast. At review, explain differences in volume, price, time, contribution and collection dates. Record whether a missed result reflects demand, delivery limits, changed assumptions or execution. Revise the next forecast using new evidence while retaining accountability for the original goal.

Use the sales-forecast method for expected demand, rolling forecasting for refreshed assumptions and the cash forecast for payment dates. Put the corrective action, responsible person, deadline and next evidence check next to the goal rather than in a separate forgotten task list.

Small-business strategic planning chooses which customers to serve, how the business will compete and where limited resources will go. A workable strategy makes trade-offs explicit, funds a few coherent priorities and defines how evidence will trigger a review.

All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business.

Start with the decision the business needs to make

Review the actual customer mix, contribution, delivery process, cash cycle and bottleneck. Separate recurring strengths from a one-time favorable month. Use customer evidence and relevant alternatives to identify where the business has a defensible advantage, rather than filling a long SWOT list with untested claims.

State the central choice in one sentence. For a fictional service company, the choice is whether to concentrate on nearby repeat office customers or pursue a wider premium project market. Both can sound attractive. The strategy must explain which one receives scarce management attention and practical delivery hours first.

Compare choices using the same scarce resource

Illustrative monthly steady-state cases, before separate setup cash
ChoiceNearby repeat officesWider premium projects
Customer volume20 accounts12 projects
Revenue per customer$500$900
Relevant delivery cost per customer$250$450

At 120 practical delivery hours, the premium-project option fully uses the stated capacity; the repeat-office option uses 100 hours. Premium projects produce $400 more monthly result under the assumptions, but lower contribution per delivery hour and no spare delivery capacity. Those facts do not automatically choose the winner: customer evidence, volatility, sales effort and execution risk remain material.

State what the business will decline or defer

If the company chooses nearby repeat offices, it might prioritize route density, consistent scope and renewal discipline, while deferring distant custom work. That choice needs evidence that the nearby market can support the volume and accepted price. The 20 unallocated hours may provide resilience or future capacity; they do not become revenue without customers.

If it chooses premium projects, it must support the longer delivery scope and potentially different sales and collection cycle. In a separate startup scenario, the repeat-office approach needs $2,000 setup cash and premium projects need $6,000. Those are original assumptions to test, not deductions from the steady-state result. Map the actual cash timing and avoid judging the choice on one monthly profit number alone.

Fund a short list of connected initiatives

For the repeat-office choice, coherent initiatives could include validating a compact service area, standardizing the service checklist and measuring renewals. Allocate hours, budget and an owner to each. Do not simultaneously approve a distant custom-sales push if it consumes the resources the chosen strategy needs.

Write a one-page action record: choice, evidence, initiative, resources, owner, deadline, outcome measure and review trigger. Connect the operating assumptions to the budget and cash forecast. A list of activities without a resource limit is not an allocation decision. Hiring, leases and other harder-to-reverse commitments need their own explicit decision case.

Use a quarterly review to challenge the choice

At the chosen review date, examine whether the customer and delivery assumptions held. Track contribution per constrained hour, customer retention, actual selling effort, collection delays and service quality. Compare matching periods and definitions. A missed target may need a tactical adjustment, a revised assumption or a different strategic choice; identify which before adding more initiatives.

The business plan explains the wider venture, rolling forecasting refreshes operating expectations and customer profitability analysis tests cost to serve. Preserve the original strategy and review evidence so the next quarter’s changes are deliberate rather than reactions to whichever new opportunity appears first.

html:
A business risk assessment identifies events that could prevent an objective, estimates their impact and likelihood over a defined horizon, and assigns a response owner. Use a risk register to turn the assessment into dated decisions, not just a colored score.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Define the objective before listing risks

Start with an observable objective: for this fictional workshop, deliver accepted jobs over the next quarter while keeping available cash above a chosen $6,000 floor. Name the horizon and which operations are included. “Economic risk” is too broad to assign; “the sole component supplier fails to deliver before a committed customer date” identifies an event, a dependency and an exposure.

Separate the cause, event and consequence. An unreliable supplier is a cause; a missed delivery is an event; replacement freight, idle labor and a delayed customer receipt are consequences. Record existing controls before estimating the remaining exposure. A business risk register can sit within enterprise risk management, but this small-business worksheet is not a certified ERM or cybersecurity standard.

Build a register that can produce an action

Original quarterly workshop risk register; ranges are management assumptions
EventAssumed probabilityImpact / cash effectProposed control costOwnerReview trigger
Supplier interruption10–20% / quarter$12,000–$20,000Backup supplier test: $600Ops leadLead time > 14 days
Customer delay15–30% / quarter$8,000 receipt shiftedMilestone verification: $200Collections leadInvoice disputed > 5 days
Equipment failure5–10% / quarter$3,000–$7,000Service/backup review: $300Workshop leadFailed inspection

The probabilities are deliberately uncertain assumptions, not observed frequencies. Add evidence dates, control status and an assessment confidence note. A control described as planned is not an effective control until implemented and tested. Keep inherent exposure and residual exposure as separate versions, with a reason for any estimated reduction.

Calculate exposure without calling it a reserve

At a selected 15% probability and $16,000 loss, the supplier event has a simple probability-weighted exposure of $2,400 per quarter. If a tested backup arrangement reduced the assumed probability to 8%, holding severity constant, exposure would be $1,280. The modeled reduction is $1,120; less a $600 control cost leaves $520 in this narrow comparison. It does not prove the control will work or that spending $600 is the best decision.

Do not multiply an ordinal “likelihood 4” by an ordinal “impact 5” and label 20 as dollars. Do not add overlapping consequences twice, such as total lost sales plus the full profit lost on those same sales. Identify which costs stop when delivery stops. Consider correlated events: one outage could delay both the supplier and the customer. A simple sum of independent-looking scores can conceal that dependency.

Stress the dated cash position separately

Suppose opening available cash is $14,000. Planned receipts of $18,000 and payments of $20,000 give $12,000 closing cash. A receipt delay of $8,000 gives $4,000, below the selected $6,000 floor by $2,000. The customer may still owe the money; moving its clearing date is a funding problem, not automatically an $8,000 permanent loss. Re-run the following periods when the receipt clears.

Combine plausible disruptions and test payment order near the low point. A probability-weighted loss cannot tell you whether payroll clears on Friday. Use the financial contingency plan for response funding and the dated cash-flow forecast for timing.

Choose, test and review the response

Compare avoiding the activity, reducing exposure, transferring a defined part or consciously accepting the residual risk. Check the actual contract or insurance scope before treating a transfer as effective. Record cost, implementation date, responsible person and evidence of a test. A second supplier that has not qualified the component is still an unresolved dependency.

Review when a trigger occurs and at a scheduled cutoff. Preserve the prior estimate so a changed forecast cannot erase the original decision. Close an action only after its evidence exists; keep the risk open if the underlying exposure remains. Tie the major unresolved conditions to the feasibility decision rather than assigning every risk a low score to justify proceeding.

faq.a: No. An ordinal ranking is a prioritization aid. A monetary expected-loss estimate needs explicit probabilities, amounts and a consistent horizon.

faq.a: Not automatically. Size the funding response using dated commitments, severe plausible scenarios and the chosen cash floor.

Choose the operating model before the platform

Consider a narrowly scoped editing service, a specialist spreadsheet template or a curated physical accessory. Each needs a defined buyer and evidence that the offer solves a problem. The service sells a delivery commitment; the download sells a usable digital asset; ecommerce adds sourcing, stock and fulfillment. These are examples to test, not a ranking of profitable opportunities.

A marketplace can supply discovery and payment tools while creating fees, competition and platform dependence. Your own site offers different control but still needs a way to attract qualified customers. Do not choose by the platform headline alone: write who buys, why, what they receive, when they pay and what you must do after the sale.

Put three models on a consistent cost boundary

ModelNet priceIncluded variable costsContributionResource constraintCash issue

Digital download$40 sale$4 delivery/support + $12 acquisition$2460 setup hours + supportRefunds and ongoing updates

The service contribution is $600 − $90 − $150 = $360, or $30 per owner-hour over twelve hours. The download leaves $24 per sale. At 100 sales, that is $2,400 before recovering setup work and fixed costs. Valuing 60 creation hours at a selected $25 adds a $1,500 planning requirement; that is an explicit owner-time assumption, not a cash invoice or market wage.

The ecommerce order contributes $16 after the included costs. A hypothetical $800 monthly fixed commitment requires 50 orders merely to cover that commitment at unchanged unit economics. Refunds, damaged stock and owner pay still need their own included or separately identified treatment. A higher revenue total can coexist with a weaker cash position.

Collect evidence matched to the model

What a small test must reveal

Digital productSmall usable sample and paid releaseBuyer can use the file; support requestsPurchase depends on misleading claims
EcommerceSmall stock batchNet receipts, returns, delivery costUnsold inventory absorbs cash

Interest is useful but not equivalent to an order. Record prospects who declined as well as buyers. A successful pilot demonstrates that one transaction worked under its conditions; it does not establish a repeatable acquisition cost or a large market. Set a test budget and decision date before seeing the result.

Trace cash before calling a model low-cost

For a separate ecommerce batch of 50 units, paying $42 goods cost per unit uses $2,100 before sales. If only 30 units sell, 20 units remain in stock. Do not expense or ignore that stock solely to make a launch cash estimate match a per-order contribution table. Shipping, acquisition, fees, refunds and settlement delays need their own dates. The startup cost calculator organizes one-time and recurring cash requirements.

A digital product avoids physical stock but can still require software, licensed materials, design effort, support and maintenance. A service may require no inventory but be capped by qualified delivery hours. Test the bottleneck that actually constrains the model.

Choose the next test rather than an earnings promise

Reject a model if you cannot deliver it competently, access the intended customers or tolerate its funding gap. Verify relevant professional and local requirements for the actual activity. Do not infer permission to offer regulated services from an idea list. Compare the best-supported alternatives in the general business-idea screen.

Write a testable offer and acceptance boundary

Specify the deliverable, exclusions, net price, turnaround, revision limits and how acceptance is recorded. For the fictional pilot here, a $300 service package takes six delivery hours and $40 job-specific cash costs. Record when the buyer can cancel and how a refund or complaint will be handled. Use the online model comparison if the model is undecided. This guide starts after that choice. It does not require a custom store: the first workflow can be simple if it supports accurate terms, appropriate records and a reliable way to fulfill the offer.

Check the activity and selling locations

SBA launch guidance separates registration, IDs, permits, banking and insurance. The IRS startup checklist is explicitly not exhaustive and points to state requirements. Record which official state and local offices apply to your actual business, where customers are served and what evidence remains outstanding. For a business operating at home, also check workspace, property and capacity constraints. For US merchandise orders, the FTC explains requirements concerning advertised shipping times, delay consent and refunds. Read the applicable rule before making a shipping promise. Verify the proposed activity at the actual address

List customer visits, employees, storage, deliveries, noise, equipment and signage before asking the relevant authority what is permitted. Arizona Commerce’s location checklist illustrates why residential zoning and property restrictions matter even for an online business. It is an Arizona reference, not permission for another city or state. Obtain current information for your actual location.

Keep a dated verification record: office contacted, activity described, response, reference number and unresolved conditions. Review lease or property restrictions and relevant insurance coverage. A quiet desk-based activity and a home food-production operation need different checks. Do not substitute a generic startup checklist for activity-specific requirements.

Design the work boundary and safe capacity

Specify a dedicated work area, storage maximum, customer handoff method and working hours. Separate business records and customer data from shared household access. Identify equipment, internet or power dependencies and the practical fallback if a failure prevents a promised delivery. Avoid counting every hour at home as productive capacity.

In this case, the owner has 56 hours available monthly, reserves 16 for administration and selling, and can deliver in the remaining 40. At two hours per completed job, that permits 20 jobs. Family commitments, interruptions and rework could lower that ceiling. Test actual completion times before accepting the maximum schedule.

Separate incremental cash from household allocations

Original home-based service budget; no tax deduction claim
ItemAmount / quantityScope
One-time equipment$900Cash before launch
Workspace adaptation$300Cash before launch
Monthly incremental commitments$350Software, utilities and cover in this case
Net price per job$120Accepted service output
Relevant cash cost per job$25Included job inputs
Contribution per job$95Before owner income and fixed costs
Practical job capacity2040 available delivery hours / 2 hours
Selected owner-income goal$1,500 / monthSeparate planning requirement

Startup cash here is $900 + $300 = $1,200. It is separate from the monthly $350 commitments. A fair-use share of existing household rent may help an internal full-cost view, but it is not necessarily an additional cash payment caused by starting. Document whether each amount is new cash, an allocation or an owner-time allowance. The treatment for a tax return is a separate question for the applicable rules and adviser.

At $95 contribution, covering $350 monthly commitments takes four whole jobs because $350 / $95 is about 3.68. Adding the separate $1,500 owner-income planning goal needs twenty jobs because $1,850 / $95 is about 19.47. That uses the entire delivery capacity. It leaves little room for rework and does not fund additional owner benefits or tax.

Test a slower job before relying on the plan

At 2.5 hours per job, forty delivery hours permit sixteen jobs. Sixteen × $95 − $350 = $1,170 toward the stated owner goal, leaving a $330 gap against $1,500. The business can cover its narrow overhead while failing the owner-income target. Do not label “above operating break-even” as “enough to support the owner.”

If all twenty jobs sell at the planned scope, $2,400 sales less $500 job cash costs and $350 commitments leaves $1,550 before the separate exclusions. Recovery of the $1,200 startup spending requires additional analysis over time; do not deduct it twice as both a one-time launch payment and monthly fixed cash.

Set a review routine before accepting more work

Reconcile accepted jobs, hours, refunds, stock if any and cleared cash weekly. Limit bookings by productive hours and property constraints, not website demand alone. Record when you will revisit price, scope, equipment or location. Expansion can create a new permit, insurance or capacity question rather than being a simple multiplication of sales.

title: Assets, Liabilities and Equity: Accounting Equation Examples
seoTitle: Assets, Liabilities and Equity: Examples
description: Follow eight reconciled transactions through assets, liabilities and equity. Separate profit, borrowing, customer collections and owner withdrawals.
metaDescription: Follow eight reconciled transactions through assets, liabilities and equity. Separate profit, borrowing, customer collections and owner withdrawals.
scopeBoundary: Accounting-equation primer, not complete statement analysis or business valuation.
opening: The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + equity. Assets show recognized resources, liabilities show obligations, and equity is the residual interest. Every recorded transaction must preserve the equality even when cash, profit and debt move differently.
alt: Symbolic balanced business resources, obligation folders and owner-capital notebook.
imageCaption: AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases.
html:
The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + equity. Assets show recognized resources, liabilities show obligations, and equity is the residual interest. Every recorded transaction must preserve the equality even when cash, profit and debt move differently.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Read the equation as a relationship, not a valuation

The SEC financial-statement guide describes the balance sheet as a snapshot. Book equity is the accounting residual; it is not a promise of the price a business could sell for. A resource can be useful without all of its economic value appearing as a recognized asset. The equation alone does not tell you whether customer demand, liquidity or future profitability is strong.

Owner investment and earned income both can increase equity but represent different activity. Borrowing increases an obligation rather than creating revenue. An owner withdrawal reduces the owner’s interest; it is not automatically an operating expense. This simplified service example uses an accrual view with no tax, inventory, depreciation, interest or other omitted period adjustments.

Trace eight transactions without losing the balance

Cumulative balances immediately after each transaction, USD
TransactionTotal assetsTotal liabilitiesEquity
Owner invests $18,000$18,000$0$18,000
Borrow $6,000$24,000$6,000$18,000
Buy $5,000 equipment for cash$24,000$6,000$18,000
Earn and invoice $4,000 service$28,000$6,000$22,000
Collect $2,500 of that invoice$28,000$6,000$22,000
Incur $1,200 unpaid expense$28,000$7,200$20,800
Pay $700 of the expense$27,300$6,500$20,800
Owner withdraws $800$26,500$6,500$20,000

Buying the equipment exchanges $5,000 cash for $5,000 equipment: total assets do not change in this simplified initial-recognition example. Earning the service creates $4,000 receivable and increases equity through income. Collecting $2,500 exchanges receivable for cash without earning the revenue again. Incurring the unpaid $1,200 expense increases liabilities and reduces equity; paying $700 later reduces cash and the liability together.

The last row balances: $26,500 = $6,500 + $20,000. An equal balance is necessary, but it does not prove that the correct accounts, period or amounts were used. Recording the same wrong amount on both sides still balances.

Reconcile the closing accounts and equity bridge

Closing account detail; check against the transaction log
Asset accountUSDLiability / equity accountUSD
Cash20,000Loan6,000
Accounts receivable1,500Unpaid expense500
Equipment5,000Owner equity20,000
Total26,500Total26,500

Cash is $18,000 + $6,000 − $5,000 + $2,500 − $700 − $800 = $20,000. Equity is $18,000 investment + $4,000 earned revenue − $1,200 expense − $800 withdrawal = $20,000. Included profit is $2,800, while cash increased $20,000 from zero because investment, borrowing and asset purchases also affect cash. Do not use the cash change as profit.

Find errors the equality will not reveal

Use source documents to confirm that a customer collection has not been recorded as new revenue. Check that a bank loan was not posted to sales and that an equipment payment was not automatically treated as an immediate period expense. Review whether an unpaid invoice belongs to the period. Each error can leave a superficially balanced ledger.

A negative equity balance is possible and needs analysis of accumulated losses, distributions and the relevant accounting basis. It is not a negative cash balance by definition. Likewise, an asset-heavy business can have little available cash. See current asset classification and current liability classification before interpreting short-term coverage.

Use the equation inside a complete close

Start from reconciled opening balances, post supported transactions, complete necessary period adjustments and compare detailed accounts with the statement totals. Retain the prior version and the reason for every correction. Do not force a difference into equity just to make the statement balance.

The AR workflow and AP workflow help support two common balances. Continue with financial statement analysis for the relationship among performance, balances and cash. This primer does not replace journal-entry policy, a full closing checklist or specialist review.

seoTitle: Current Assets: Classification and Example
description: Classify cash, receivables, inventory and prepayments at one reporting date. Reconcile a current-assets schedule and separate its total from available cash.
metaDescription: Classify cash, receivables, inventory and prepayments at one reporting date. Reconcile a current-assets schedule and separate its total from available cash.
scopeBoundary: Classification only; working-capital and ratio guides retain their calculations.
opening: Current assets are assets expected to be realized or consumed within the applicable short-term classification period, commonly one year or the normal operating cycle if longer. Classify and measure each balance before adding it; current does not mean immediately spendable cash.
alt: Organized current asset records, boxed inventory and prepaid coverage folder in a retail back office.

html:
Current assets are assets expected to be realized or consumed within the applicable short-term classification period, commonly one year or the normal operating cycle if longer. Classify and measure each balance before adding it; current does not mean immediately spendable cash.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Start with dates and restrictions

Use the actual reporting basis and operating cycle. A routine retailer’s inventory may be current even though it has not sold, while equipment used for several years is normally outside this category. For this fictional short-cycle business, all included inventory and prepayments relate to the next twelve months. Unusual operating cycles and restricted balances require policy-specific review.

Ask what the asset is, when it is expected to be realized or used, what restriction applies and what supports its carrying amount. A label in a software account is not sufficient evidence. Principlesofaccounting’s classified-balance-sheet lesson explains the one-year or longer operating-cycle boundary; this schedule is an original application, not a universal classification ruling.

Reconcile a same-date current-assets schedule

Original reporting-date classification, USD
BalanceAmountClassificationEvidence
Available cash$12,000CurrentReconciled bank/cash records
Gross trade receivables$9,000Current before allowanceCustomer invoice ledger
Receivable allowance−$600Reduces carrying amountDocumented assessment
Inventory$7,000Current in this caseCount and cost records
Prepaid insurance consumed in next 12 months$1,200CurrentPolicy dates
Total current assets$28,600Sum onceSame reporting date
Equipment carrying amount$15,000NoncurrentFixed-asset schedule
Long-term restricted deposit$2,000Noncurrent in this caseRestriction over 12 months

The current total is $12,000 + $9,000 − $600 + $7,000 + $1,200 = $28,600. Net receivables are $8,400. Do not add both $9,000 gross receivables and $8,400 net receivables. The allowance is a reduction of the carrying amount, not an additional bank account or a customer credit note.

The $15,000 equipment and $2,000 deposit excluded from current assets remain relevant to total assets. In this deliberately limited schedule, total listed assets are $45,600. Excluding them from one subtotal does not remove them from the balance sheet.

Separate current assets from cash available for payments

Only the stated $12,000 is currently available cash in the example. Receivables need collection; inventory needs sale and settlement; prepaid insurance supplies future coverage rather than cash to pay a supplier. The $28,600 subtotal therefore cannot be read as the amount available for tomorrow’s payroll.

Prepare a separate dated view. If $5,000 of receivables clears next week and $3,000 stock requires a slow sales cycle, list those events on their expected dates. Do not invent a collection date from the fact that an item is current. Review customer disputes and stock condition before treating all balances as equally recoverable.

Check measurement without double-counting adjustments

Reconcile cash to statements, the customer detail to the control account and physical stock to inventory records. Assess returns, damage, expiry and valuation under the applicable policy. Check the unused period on each prepayment. A prepaid annual bill should not remain at its original full amount after some of the coverage has been consumed.

For a separate sensitivity, reducing this example’s inventory carrying amount by $1,000 would reduce current assets from $28,600 to $27,600, all else unchanged. It does not create a $1,000 cash payment on the adjustment date. Do not deduct the same adjustment again if the listed inventory is already net of it.

Use the classification in the next decision

Compare the category with current liabilities at the same cutoff. The working-capital guide owns the defined difference; the financial-ratios hub owns ratio interpretation. This article supplies account classification, not a recommended ratio or cash reserve.

Use invoice and collection records to explain the receivable balance and the accounting equation to reconcile total assets with obligations and equity. Keep the reporting schedule and cash forecast connected without pretending they answer the same question.

title: Current Liabilities: Classify Obligations and Due Dates
seoTitle: Current Liabilities: Examples and Due Dates
description: Classify supplier bills, payroll accruals, advances and current debt. Reconcile a liability schedule and separate recognition from cash payment dates.
metaDescription: Classify supplier bills, payroll accruals, advances and current debt. Reconcile a liability schedule and separate recognition from cash payment dates.
scopeBoundary: Liability classification; detailed AP processing and ratio formulas retain separate owners.
opening: Current liabilities are obligations classified as short term under the applicable accounting rules, commonly due within one year or the normal operating cycle. Build the total from supported balances, then create a separate due-date schedule for cash planning.
alt: Finance coordinator arranging supplier, payroll and loan obligations along a payment planner.
imageCaption: AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases.
html:
Current liabilities are obligations classified as short term under the applicable accounting rules, commonly due within one year or the normal operating cycle. Build the total from supported balances, then create a separate due-date schedule for cash planning.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Distinguish recognition from the next payment date

An obligation can exist before the supplier sends its invoice. A payment can settle an old obligation without becoming a new expense. Some obligations, such as customer advances, may be settled by delivering goods or services rather than paying the same amount in cash. These differences matter when converting a balance sheet to a cash plan.

OpenStax describes common current-liability categories, including payables, accrued wages, unearned revenue and current debt portions. Debt terms, covenant issues, refinancing and unusual operating cycles can require specialized classification analysis. This simplified example assumes no such complications; it does not determine treatment for a particular loan.

Add each obligation once at the reporting cutoff

Original classification schedule, USD
ObligationBalanceSupporting evidence
Trade accounts payable$8,000Supplier terms / invoice due dates
Accrued payroll$2,500Earned before cutoff; payable next run
Other accrued expense$900Service received; not duplicated in AP
Tax collected / payable$1,100Separate obligation; verify due dates
Customer advance$2,000Undelivered service next month
Current portion of loan principal$3,000Contractually due in next 12 months
Total current liabilities$17,500Same cutoff
Remaining long-term loan principal$9,000Noncurrent in this simplified case

The current total is $8,000 + $2,500 + $900 + $1,100 + $2,000 + $3,000 = $17,500. The loan balance is $12,000 in total: $3,000 current and $9,000 noncurrent in this case. Adding the entire $12,000 again to current liabilities would duplicate the current portion and misclassify the rest.

The $900 accrued expense is explicitly outside the supplier ledger here. When an invoice for that same service is posted, reconcile or reverse the accrual under the accounting policy. Leaving both as independent obligations would overstate the total. A disputed invoice still needs an assessment; withholding payment alone does not decide whether a liability exists.

Turn the balance into a payment calendar carefully

Separate near-term settlement illustration
ItemCash due within next 30 daysOther settlement
Supplier bills5,0003,000 later
Payroll2,500None in this case
Accrued service900None
Tax amount1,100Check actual statutory date
Loan principal250Remaining current principal later
Customer advanceNot assumed to be 2,000 cash outflowDeliver the service; refund conditions reviewed
Listed 30-day cash total9,750Not the 17,500 liability total

The $9,750 is the sum of the listed near-term payments, not all costs of fulfilling the advance and not the whole next-month business budget. Add relevant future service-delivery cash and other commitments separately. Do not add the $2,000 advance as both an automatic cash repayment and all fulfillment costs unless the actual scenario requires both.

Investigate omissions before interpreting coverage

Review goods or services received near the cutoff, payroll earned but unpaid, lender schedules, customer advances and tax control accounts. Match supplier statements to detail and document differences. Check whether a credit note has been posted and whether payments in transit are represented consistently. A low payable balance can reflect an omitted bill rather than strong finances.

Current classification and overdue status answer different questions. A bill due next month and a bill overdue for sixty days can both be current. Maintain due dates, dispute status and payment evidence so a single balance cannot hide urgent exceptions.

Connect classification to cash and account workflows

Use the AP approval and reconciliation workflow for supplier records. Compare with current asset classifications at the same date before using working capital or a ratio. A positive subtotal difference does not prove that cash arrives before the bills.

The accounting equation example separates borrowing from profit. The cash-flow forecast uses payment and collection dates. Keep forecast commitments that are not yet recognized liabilities visibly separate from the accounting total.

faq.a: Not necessarily. Current classification is a reporting category; overdue status depends on the agreed due date.

faq.a: No. Some customer advances are settled through delivery. Assess actual fulfillment and refund obligations.

The accounts receivable process tracks customer amounts from a valid invoice through credits, collections and reconciliation. Keep each invoice, due date, receipt allocation and open balance connected so the total can be explained from individual customer records.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Agree the terms and evidence before billing

Record the customer identity, approved scope, delivery or acceptance evidence, invoice contact and agreed payment terms. Establish who can approve a credit change or adjustment. An invoice date is not proof that the full revenue-recognition criteria were met; the accounting basis and delivery facts still matter.

JPMorgan’s receivables guidance describes the broad sequence from credit assessment through cash application and reconciliation. This article supplies a small original invoice ledger, not an assessment of customer creditworthiness or a debt-collection legal procedure. Use appropriate professional support for disputed obligations and regulated collection activity.

Keep a reconciled invoice-level record

Original gross customer ledger; no tax, allowance or write-off in this case
InvoiceInvoice dateDue dateInvoiceApplied cashCreditOpenStatus on Nov 6
A-101Oct 1Oct 31$5,000$2,000$0$3,0006 days overdue
A-102Oct 20Nov 19$4,000$0$500$3,500Not yet due
A-103Sep 15Oct 15$3,000$1,000$0$2,00022 days overdue
TotalAs of Nov 6, 2026Due-date aging$12,000$3,000$500$8,500Reconcile to control account

Open gross receivables are $12,000 invoices − $3,000 allocated collections − $500 approved credit = $8,500. A-102’s credit reduces its balance to $3,500; it is not a $500 receipt. Record the credit’s reason and approval. This ledger does not include an expected-credit-loss allowance; a financial-statement carrying amount may need a separate supported adjustment.

Check every customer row and the overall movement. At an opening gross AR of $7,000, new invoices of $5,000, collections of $3,000 and credits of $500 produce the same $8,500 closing control balance. The movement is a separate summary of this month’s activity, not a second set of invoices to add to the ledger.

Age balances using one explicit date policy

Using due dates and a November 6 cutoff, A-101 is six days overdue, A-103 twenty-two days overdue and A-102 not yet due. Thus $5,000 is 1–30 days overdue and $3,500 is not yet due. The aging total is $8,500. A report aged from invoice date would show different buckets, so label the basis before comparing reports.

Separate disputes, promises to pay and collection estimates from posted cash. A customer email promising $2,000 does not reduce the open balance. Assign a dispute owner, required evidence and next contact date. Preserve the original terms and any approved change; do not rewrite a due date simply to improve the aging report.

Match the receipt without earning revenue twice

For A-101, apply the $2,000 receipt to that invoice and retain its bank reference. A general transfer from a customer may need remittance evidence before allocating across several invoices. Keep unidentified receipts visible for investigation under the accounting policy instead of guessing an allocation.

If a processor settles $970 against a supported $1,000 invoice and withholds a documented $30 fee, the settlement may require $970 cash plus $30 fee to clear the $1,000 receivable. Do not leave a fictional $30 customer debt or reduce sales without examining the actual settlement. Refunds, withholding and currency differences need their own documented treatment.

Reconcile detail, control account and bank evidence

At cutoff, total the customer detail and compare it with the general-ledger AR control account. Explain manual journals, unapplied cash, credits, duplicates and timing differences. Separately reconcile bank activity. An AR ledger cannot equal the bank balance because it represents unpaid amounts rather than cash held.

Re-run the detail after corrections, retain the reconciliation and have an appropriate reviewer investigate unresolved differences. Feed expected clearing dates into the cash forecast. For definitions use current assets; for the customer-versus-supplier distinction use AR versus AP. The AP workflow handles money owed to suppliers, without netting unrelated customers and vendors.

The accounts payable process verifies supplier obligations, records approved invoices and credits, schedules authorized payments and reconciles the remaining balance. Match what was ordered, received and billed before paying, and preserve evidence for exceptions.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Capture the invoice and validate the supplier record

Use a controlled intake location and record supplier, invoice number, currency, date, terms, purchase reference and total. Check duplicates using more than a file name: the same bill can arrive as a PDF, reminder and statement. A supplier statement summarizes activity; it is not automatically a new expense.

Separate supplier-detail changes, invoice approval and payment release where practical. Verify a requested bank-detail change through a previously trusted contact route, not only the new email. In a very small business, an independent owner review of the evidence can compensate for limited staffing, but it should be an actual recorded check.

Match receipt and price, then resolve exceptions

Microsoft’s invoice-matching documentation distinguishes price comparison with the purchase order from the additional receipt-quantity check. Choose controls that fit the purchase. A service may need approved completion evidence instead of a warehouse receipt; a non-PO bill needs a documented authorization route, not automatic approval.

For an independent goods example, a purchase order requests 100 components at $20, but the receiving record shows only 90 accepted. A supplier invoice for $2,000 raises a $200 quantity exception. Investigate the missing ten and request correction or evidence before approval. Do not silently change the receipt to 100 to make the documents agree. Recognition of goods received and treatment of any dispute still follow the accounting policy.

Reconcile the supplier balances and monthly movement

Original gross AP detail; no tax, foreign exchange or unresolved accrual in this case

V-201Oct 15Nov 14$4,000$1,500$0$2,500Receiving checked

The ledger closes at $9,000 invoices − $2,500 allocated payments − $300 approved credit = $6,200. V-203’s remaining $1,000 is twelve days overdue on November 6. The credit on V-202 is not a payment; retain the supplier reference and reason. A dispute flag is not permission to delete a supported obligation.

The separate month movement is $4,500 opening AP + $4,500 new bills − $2,500 payments − $300 credits = $6,200. Compare that result with the supplier-detail total and GL control balance. Do not add the opening balances to a closing ledger that already includes them.

Authorize the payment without duplicating the expense

Prepare a proposed payment run with invoice references, due dates, available cash and hold reasons. Review agreed discounts against actual terms; do not assume delaying every payment improves the business. A planned payment is not a completed bank transaction. Retain release approval and settlement evidence, then allocate the payment to the correct invoice.

If $1,500 of V-201 is paid after that invoice was already recorded, reduce cash and the payable. Posting another $1,500 expense at payment would duplicate the cost. A purchase can instead relate to inventory, equipment or a prepayment, so the AP workflow must not force every bill into operating expense.

Close with supplier, ledger and cutoff checks

Compare supplier statements with internal invoices, payments and credits. Investigate missing invoices, unallocated payments, duplicates and payments in transit. Reconcile supplier detail to the AP control account at the same cutoff. Review received goods and completed services not yet invoiced, keeping necessary accruals separate until matched so they are not counted twice.

Use liability classification for the reporting boundary and the customer collection workflow for incoming amounts. The AR-versus-AP comparison explains the distinction. Feed actual supplier due dates into the cash plan; a reconciled $6,200 balance does not itself say which payments are due tomorrow.

Accrual accounting records revenue and expenses in the periods to which they belong under the accounting framework, rather than using cash dates alone. Separate the delivery, billing and settlement evidence before comparing profit with a bank balance.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Identify what happened before choosing the date

For this introductory financial-reporting example, assume an accepted service gives an unconditional right to payment and all relevant recognition conditions are satisfied in November. The invoice is issued later. The invoice date by itself does not determine when revenue is earned. If payment depends on additional performance, a contract asset or another treatment may be relevant; do not automatically call every unbilled amount accounts receivable.

Likewise, distinguish a service consumed, an asset purchased and an advance paid. A December payment for November work can settle an existing obligation. Insurance paid in advance can provide coverage over several periods. These distinctions organize the evidence; they are not an election of a permissible US tax method.

Use four transactions with separate accounting and cash dates

Original November 2026 accrual case; USD
EventNovember recognitionCash / billing dateIllustrative posting
Accepted November service; unconditional payment right$5,000 earned in NovemberInvoice Dec 1; collect Dec 15Dr receivable / Cr revenue 5,000
November payroll earned$1,800 November expensePay December 5Dr wage expense / Cr payable 1,800
Insurance paid November 1; twelve months coverage$100 November expense; $1,100 prepaid$1,200 November paymentDr insurance expense / Cr prepaid 100 at close
Customer advance for December serviceNo November revenue from this advance$2,400 November receiptDr cash / Cr contract liability 2,400

The insurance initially creates a $1,200 prepaid asset. One month of coverage is then consumed, leaving $1,100. The $2,400 advance is assumed refundable or deliverable under the contract and wholly unearned at November 30. It is not extra November sales merely because money arrived. No sales tax, bad-debt adjustment, depreciation or other expenses are included in this deliberately limited example.

Reconcile November profit, cash and balances

Earned revenue is $5,000. Included expenses are $1,800 payroll plus $100 insurance, so accrual profit is $3,100. Operating receipts less payments in this case are $2,400 − $1,200 = $1,200. The $1,900 difference between profit and this operating cash movement is explained by $5,000 new receivable, $1,100 remaining prepaid, $1,800 unpaid wages and $2,400 customer advance: $3,100 − $5,000 − $1,100 + $1,800 + $2,400 = $1,200.

Add a separate $10,000 owner cash investment at the beginning. Closing cash becomes $11,200, not $3,100. Assets are $11,200 cash + $5,000 receivable + $1,100 prepaid = $17,300. Liabilities are $1,800 wages + $2,400 advance = $4,200. Equity is $10,000 investment + $3,100 profit = $13,100. Thus $17,300 = $4,200 + $13,100.

This is a financial-reporting illustration. A simple cash receipts/payments view of these transactions is not a complete tax-basis income computation. Loan principal, equipment purchases, deposits, constructive receipt and applicable tax rules can require additional analysis.

Carry the balances into December without counting twice

On December 15, collecting the $5,000 reduces the receivable and increases cash; it does not recognize the same service revenue again. Paying $1,800 wages settles the November payable. Consuming another month of insurance reduces the prepaid asset by another $100. Recognize the advance as earned only when the assumed December service conditions are satisfied, not automatically because the calendar changed.

Preserve references from each settlement to its original transaction. Use the receivable workflow for collection allocation and the liability schedule for unpaid obligations. A balanced entry can still contain the wrong period or classification.

Use a cutoff review before reading the result

At month end, inspect accepted work, invoices issued before or after cutoff, services received but unbilled, unused prepayments and unfulfilled customer promises. Document the reporting basis and reviewer. Reconcile opening balances plus movements to closing schedules; do not replace missing evidence with an arbitrary journal to make profit look reasonable.

The accounting cycle connects adjustments to statements. Bookkeeping for small business covers the routine evidence collection, and the cash forecast handles future payment timing. IRS Publication 538 is the separate official reference for tax accounting methods; this guide makes no blanket eligibility or change-of-method claim.

Small-business bookkeeping turns supported transactions into consistent records and reconciled balances. A useful monthly routine collects evidence, posts transactions once, resolves differences and preserves a reviewed closing package.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Build the record around evidence rather than the bank feed

Keep an identifiable link between each posting and the underlying sale, supplier bill, receipt, payroll record or agreement. The IRS describes supporting business documents as the evidence behind entries. Its tax-record guidance is not a substitute for your financial-reporting policy, but it reinforces why a bank description alone may not explain what a transaction represents.

Assign a unique reference, reporting date, amount, currency, counterparty and account. Separate business and personal activity appropriately. A bank feed entry can match an invoice payment already recorded; importing it as another sale would duplicate income. Keep unidentified items in a visible investigation list rather than assigning convenient categories.

Separate daily capture from the monthly close

A practical sequence with observable completion evidence
FrequencyWorkEvidence of completion
Daily / weeklyCollect and match documents; post invoices and paymentsUnique references; no unexplained duplicates
WeeklyReview customer and supplier open itemsDetail reconciles to control accounts
Month endReconcile cash, cards, loans and relevant stockDated schedules with differences explained
Month endReview accruals, prepayments and asset schedulesApproved adjustments linked to evidence
CloseReview reports and preserve the versionReviewer, unresolved issues and next actions

Frequency depends on transaction volume and commitments, not a universal deadline invented by this guide. A business with payroll this week may need cash review before the formal month-end close. The formal close should use a consistent cutoff across reports.

Reconcile a bank difference without inventing a plug

Original cash-reconciliation case, USD
Record / adjustmentAmountReason
Cash book before omitted bank fee$9,7508,000 opening + 6,200 receipts − 4,450 payments
Unrecorded bank fee−$50Post supported fee once
Adjusted cash book$9,700Agrees to adjusted bank evidence

Outstanding payment−$400Already in books; absent from bank
Adjusted statement$9,7009,850 + 250 − 400

The $50 fee is missing from the books, so it needs a supported book entry. The $250 deposit and $400 outstanding payment are already recorded in the books; adding or subtracting them there again would duplicate their effects. Their role is to explain the statement timing. Both adjusted views reach $9,700.

An equal result does not validate every payment. Verify the recipient, amount and business purpose. Investigate old reconciling items and retain evidence of later clearing. Do not force unexplained differences into fees or owner equity.

Reconcile detail before accepting the report totals

In a separate customer subledger example, $3,000 opening receivables + $6,000 invoices − $5,200 allocated collections = $3,800 closing gross receivables. If the GL says $3,600, identify the $200 difference before treating the report as reconciled. Check credits, manual journals, duplicate invoices and unapplied receipts. This is independent of the bank example’s total receipts.

Use AR records and AP records for their respective workflows. Match asset cost and accumulated depreciation to an asset register. Check prepayment periods and accrued obligations. An account can reconcile mathematically while its valuation or classification still needs review.

Preserve the close and the unresolved-action list

Review unusual balances and changes against actual operations. Retain the trial balance, reconciliations, adjustment support and reports with their cutoff date. Assign an owner and deadline to each remaining issue. A lock date is useful only when corrections are still made through a controlled, documented process rather than silently changing prior reports.

The general ledger template supplies posting references and account-level balances; the accounting cycle explains adjustments and closing. The statement-analysis guide addresses interpretation after the records are prepared. Check the actual retention requirements for each document type; this article does not assert a single period for every business record.

html:
The accounting cycle connects transaction evidence to journal entries, ledger accounts, adjustments, statements and closing. Keep the unadjusted, adjusted and post-closing balances separate so each stage has a traceable purpose.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Record six supported events before adjusting

This fictional sole-proprietor service business begins with zero balances. The owner invests $10,000 cash. It buys $900 supplies on account, earns and invoices $4,000 of accepted services, collects $2,500 of that receivable, pays $600 rent for the month, and receives $1,200 for future services. No tax, depreciation, inventory for resale or owner drawings are included.

Journal entries preserve the two-sided effect of each event. For example, supplies purchased on account debit Supplies and credit Accounts Payable by $900. Collecting $2,500 debits Cash and credits Accounts Receivable; it does not record another sale. Post each journal reference into the appropriate ledger accounts.

Keep the adjustment evidence distinct

At month end, a supported count shows $600 supplies remain, so $300 has been used. Employees have earned $700 unpaid wages. Of the $1,200 advance, $400 is now earned under the case’s service-recognition assumptions. Record three adjustments: Dr Supplies Expense / Cr Supplies $300; Dr Wages Expense / Cr Wages Payable $700; Dr Customer Advance Liability / Cr Service Revenue $400.

These entries change the period’s result and balances without creating a cash transaction at the adjustment date. Preserve the count, payroll cutoff and delivery evidence. Adjusting to a desired profit number is not a valid substitute for that support.

The unadjusted trial balance totals $16,100 on each side. After adjustments, both sides total $16,800. Equal totals show posting equality, not proof that the right accounts and periods were used. An omitted event or a wrong but balanced entry can escape this test.

Prepare statements from the adjusted balances

Recognized revenue is $4,400. Expenses are $600 rent + $300 supplies + $700 wages = $1,600, leaving $2,800 profit. Closing equity before any drawings is $10,000 investment + $2,800 profit = $12,800. Assets are $13,100 cash + $1,500 receivables + $600 supplies = $15,200. Liabilities are $900 AP + $700 wages + $800 unearned advance = $2,400. The balance sheet reconciles: $15,200 = $2,400 + $12,800.

Cash increased $13,100 from zero, which differs from profit because owner funding, collections, credit purchases and the customer advance have different effects. The cash-flow statement and reporting framework require their own classification; do not copy the profit subtotal into a cash balance.

Close temporary accounts without deleting history

For this illustrative sole-proprietor closing convention, debit Revenue $4,400 and credit Income Summary. Debit Income Summary $1,600 and credit the three expense accounts. Transfer the remaining $2,800 credit from Income Summary to Owner Capital. Revenue, expenses and Income Summary then have zero balances; capital is $12,800. There are no drawings to close in this case.

The post-closing trial balance contains $15,200 debit assets and $15,200 credit liabilities/equity. Real systems may automate closing or use different equity accounts; do not post these manual entries on top of an automated close. Preserve the transaction history and the reports used for approval.

Use each report for its own question

The journal explains what was recorded; the ledger groups postings by account. The trial balance checks aggregate equality; the statements report the resulting position and performance. The bookkeeping routine gathers evidence and reconciles detail. Accrual accounting explains why dates can differ.

Keep the prior period’s closing balances as the next period’s opening balances and record correction references. Use statement analysis after the close to interpret the result, rather than treating interpretation as another posting step.

Use one account identity and one balance convention

The downloadable HTML template is editable and printable. It includes a completed Cash ledger and a blank working record with evidence and reviewer fields. It does not automatically calculate, post journals, create a trial balance or save edits. This limitation is deliberate: users must verify each result rather than assuming a blank manual template is an accounting application.

Set the account name/number, period, currency, opening balance and normal side. For a debit-balance account, running balance equals opening balance + debits − credits. A credit-balance account can instead use opening credit balance + credits − debits. Label the sign convention. Depreciation allocates a depreciable asset’s cost over its estimated useful life under the reporting policy. Choose a method that reflects the expected consumption pattern; depreciation is not a direct estimate of market value or a cash reserve for replacement.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Define the asset and depreciable amount first

Start with supported capitalized cost, the date the asset is available for its intended use, useful life, residual value and the relevant consumption pattern. Distinguish repairs and period expenses from costs that meet capitalization requirements. Do not classify an item as an asset only because you prefer a smaller current expense.

The original example uses equipment with $14,000 capitalized cost, $2,000 estimated residual value and a five-year useful life. The depreciable amount is $12,000. The example assumes a full first year available for use, no impairment, revaluation, disposal or estimate change, and USD financial-reporting amounts. It is not a tax-depreciation election or industry life recommendation.

Compare methods on exactly the same starting asset

Original first-year comparison; three alternative policies, not cumulative charges
MethodYear-one allocationClosing carrying amountCalculation
Straight line$2,400$11,60012,000 depreciable base / 5 years
Units of production$3,000$11,00012,000 / 60,000 units × 15,000 units
Double declining balance$5,600$8,40040% × 14,000 opening carrying amount

Straight line allocates $2,400 in each full year under unchanged estimates. Units of production uses a selected total life output of 60,000 units and first-year output of 15,000: $12,000 / 60,000 × 15,000 = $3,000. The 40% double-declining rate is twice the five-year straight-line rate and applies to opening carrying amount. Residual value is enforced as a floor; it is not subtracted again before applying that rate.

Do not add the three charges. They are alternative methods for the same asset. Their different first-year amounts reflect different assumed consumption patterns, not three separate costs to post.

Test whether the method fits the consumption evidence

A reasonably even time-based consumption pattern may support straight line. A measurable usage relationship may support units of production when output records and lifetime capacity estimates are credible. A declining pattern requires support for higher earlier consumption; choosing it only to lower reported profit is not a method-selection argument.

For the declining-balance illustration, full-year charges are $5,600, $3,360, $2,016, $1,024 and $0 after capping at the $2,000 residual. Total allocation is $12,000. The fourth year’s uncapped 40% amount would exceed the remaining depreciable amount, so it is limited. Another documented policy might switch methods; this schedule assumes no switch.

Separate expense, inventory, cash and carrying amount

If revenue before depreciation is $30,000 and other included period expenses are $20,000, the pre-depreciation result is $10,000. Treating all depreciation as a period expense in this simplified service case gives results of $7,600, $7,000 or $4,400 under the three alternatives. The asset acquisition cash payment is the same $14,000 in all three cases; the allocation itself does not pay another $2,400, $3,000 or $5,600.

In production settings, depreciation can enter manufacturing overhead and inventory before reaching cost of goods sold. Do not force every asset’s depreciation into a separate current OPEX line. Reconcile the actual capitalization and expense policy. The COGS guide retains its cost boundary.

Maintain estimates and keep the specialist schedules separate

Document the selected method, estimate evidence, reviewer and effective date. Review a change in expected life, residual amount or use under the relevant accounting framework; do not erase prior history or call every revision an error. Impairment and disposal are different questions and can change the carrying amount outside ordinary depreciation.

Use the straight-line tutorial for partial periods and a complete dated schedule. Use the accumulated-depreciation rollforward for balances and asset removals. The accounting cycle shows where supported adjustments enter statements. html:
Accumulated depreciation is the cumulative depreciation recorded against an asset or asset group that remains on the books. Reconcile opening balance, current allocations and removals separately from gross asset cost to explain the closing carrying amount.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Distinguish the period allocation from the balance

Depreciation expense or capitalized depreciation is a current-period movement. Accumulated depreciation is a balance at a date. Gross cost and accumulated depreciation generally remain separate in a cost-model asset register; their difference supports carrying amount, subject to other relevant adjustments. Accumulated depreciation is not a liability owed to a supplier.

This fictional rollforward assumes a cost model, no impairment, revaluation, foreign exchange, transfers or estimate changes. The stated $6,000 allocation has all been treated as period expense for simplicity and includes depreciation through the disposal date. A manufacturing asset register can require a separate inventory-cost reconciliation.

Reconcile gross cost and accumulated depreciation independently

Original asset-group rollforward, USD
LineAmount / balance
Opening gross asset cost50,000
Additions at supported cost10,000
Disposed asset cost removed−12,000
Closing gross asset cost48,000
Opening accumulated depreciation18,000 credit
Current period depreciation6,000 credit movement
Accumulated depreciation removed on disposal8,400 debit movement
Closing accumulated depreciation15,600 credit
Closing carrying amount32,400

Gross cost closes at $50,000 + $10,000 − $12,000 = $48,000. Accumulated depreciation closes at $18,000 + $6,000 − $8,400 = $15,600. The resulting carrying amount is $48,000 − $15,600 = $32,400. Adding the $6,000 again to closing accumulated depreciation would duplicate the period allocation.

The opening carrying amount was $32,000. Add $10,000 cost, subtract $6,000 depreciation and subtract the disposed asset’s $3,600 carrying amount: $32,000 + $10,000 − $6,000 − $3,600 = $32,400. The gross and net reconciliations agree.

Remove both the disposed cost and its accumulated balance

The disposed asset has $12,000 cost and $8,400 accumulated depreciation at sale, leaving $3,600 carrying amount. Suppose it sells for $4,000 with no selling costs. The illustrative entry debits Cash $4,000 and Accumulated Depreciation $8,400, credits Asset Cost $12,000 and Gain on Disposal $400. Debits and credits both total $12,400.

The $4,000 receipt is sale proceeds, not all gain. The $8,400 debit removes the disposed asset’s contra balance; it is not negative current depreciation. If only cost were removed, the remaining register would retain depreciation belonging to an asset no longer held. If the period allocation already runs through the disposal date, do not record it a second time.

Tie the rollforward to individual asset evidence

Assign a durable asset ID to cost, in-use date, method, life, residual value, accumulated balance and disposal record. Reconcile opening IDs plus additions less removals to the closing register. Check fully depreciated assets still used: they may remain in the register until disposal, with cost offset by accumulated depreciation under the policy.

A total can reconcile while a disposed asset remains wrongly assigned to an active location. Verify ownership, use and disposal approvals as well as arithmetic. Do not infer a gain, loss or impairment solely from a low carrying amount. Those conclusions require separate transaction and valuation evidence.

Use a balance reconciliation for the right decision

Use the methods overview when evaluating the consumption pattern. Use the straight-line schedule to compute a method-specific time allocation. The ledger template supports posting references, while the close workflow connects the register to statements.

This article explains a financial-reporting balance. Tax basis, accumulated tax depreciation and proceeds treatment may differ and are not determined here. Preserve both schedules when required rather than overwriting financial-statement balances with tax amounts.

html:
Straight-line depreciation allocates the depreciable amount evenly across the selected time-based useful life. Annual allocation equals cost minus residual value, divided by life in years; a partial-period schedule must use an explicit start date and time convention.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Define cost, life, residual and in-use date

For this independent service-asset case, capitalized cost is $14,000, residual value $2,000 and useful life five years. The asset is available for intended use on April 1, 2027. The example adopts a whole-month convention beginning that date and assumes no impairment, disposal, method switch or estimate change. These are teaching assumptions, not mandatory asset lives or a universal partial-month rule.

The purchase invoice can precede readiness for use. Keep evidence of the in-use date and explain any capitalization policy. Tax conventions can differ from this financial-reporting month count; do not automatically apply a tax half-year or mid-quarter convention to this schedule.

Compute the annual and monthly amounts once

Depreciable amount = $14,000 − $2,000 = $12,000. Annual straight-line depreciation = $12,000 / 5 = $2,400. Monthly amount = $2,400 / 12 = $200. Equivalently, $12,000 / 60 months = $200 per month. The full-year rate is 20% of the depreciable amount, not 20% of cost without considering residual value.

April through December includes nine months under the stated convention, so 2027 allocation is $200 × 9 = $1,800. Nine months is not a universal rule for every April purchase; it follows this exact in-use date and policy.

The six calendar rows cover only five years of useful life: 9 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 3 = 60 months. Four full intervening calendar years allocate $9,600. The first $1,800 and final $600 complete the $12,000 depreciable amount. Closing carrying amount stops at the $2,000 residual; do not charge another full $2,400 in 2032.

Post the allocation without inventing another cash payment

If the first nine months are all period expense in this service example, debit Depreciation Expense and credit Accumulated Depreciation by $1,800 for 2027. The original asset cost remains $14,000, accumulated depreciation becomes $1,800 and carrying amount is $12,200. No cash leaves the bank merely because that entry is posted.

Production assets may contribute depreciation to inventory costs instead. The example does not prescribe that classification for every business. Keep acquisition cash, capitalization, current allocation and eventual expense recognition traceable rather than automatically treating them as one payment.

Handle changes and rounding with a documented policy

Reassess estimates when supported facts change. A change in remaining life or residual value may change future allocation; do not silently rewrite old months or automatically treat an estimate revision as an error. An actual disposal or impairment also requires its own analysis. Use the applicable framework and approval process.

For a monthly amount that is not exact to cents, retain calculation precision and reconcile the final allocation to the intended residual. Do not round every input repeatedly and then allow the schedule to drift below its floor. This worksheet is manual and does not enforce that check automatically.

Keep the method tutorial separate from the balance rollforward

The depreciation overview compares time, usage and declining patterns. The accumulated-depreciation guide reconciles additions, current allocations and removals. The bookkeeping close provides the recurring review routine.

Record your cost evidence, readiness date, life, residual, convention and reviewer in the downloadable schedule. If any is unknown, the result is provisional; a precise formula cannot supply missing business evidence.
