html:
An allowance for doubtful accounts reduces gross receivables to a supported carrying amount for expected credit losses. Estimate the required closing balance, then reconcile the existing allowance before calculating the provision; the required balance is not automatically this period’s expense.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

State the reporting framework and current policy choices

This educational example uses US GAAP credit-loss terminology for ordinary trade receivables. It is not a complete ASC 326 model or a substitute for entity-specific accounting review. Aging percentages are fictional assumptions, not prescribed rates. Assess relevant experience, current conditions, customer-specific evidence and the applicable forecasting requirements.

FASB ASU 2025-05 introduced optional simplifications for in-scope current receivables and contract assets. A current-conditions practical expedient and, for qualifying nonpublic entities using it, a subsequent-collections policy election require their own scope and disclosure assessment. The example below assumes neither election. Do not infer that every entity must use the same forecast or subsequent-cash treatment.

Build the closing estimate from a defined receivables population

Original November 30 aging illustration; USD, due-date buckets
BucketGross balanceAssumed loss rateEstimated allowance
Not past due50,0001%500
1–30 days past due20,0004%800
Over 30 days past due10,00015%1,500
Total gross receivables80,000Illustrative rates only2,800 required closing allowance

The three amounts reconcile to $80,000 gross AR. The required closing allowance is $500 + $800 + $1,500 = $2,800, giving a $77,200 net carrying amount. Review whether similar risk characteristics support the grouping and whether any balance needs separate assessment. Avoid applying both a pooled rate and a second specific allowance to the same exposure without reconciling the overlap.

A bucket percentage must have a defensible basis and an update process in a real model. The arithmetic alone does not establish a compliant loss estimate. Preserve how credits, disputes, write-offs and subsequent evidence affect the population and rates.

Reconcile the existing allowance before recording the provision

Original allowance movement before and after estimation, USD credit-positive convention
Movement / targetAmount
Opening allowance credit1,200
Write-offs debited to allowance−700
Reinstatement on recovery+200
Credit balance before new provision700
Required closing allowance2,800
Current provision credit needed2,100

Opening credit $1,200 − $700 write-offs + $200 recovery reinstatement leaves $700 credit before the new provision. To reach $2,800, record a $2,100 provision: Dr Credit Loss / Bad Debt Expense, Cr Allowance. Recording the entire $2,800 as new expense would overstate this example’s provision by $700.

If the pre-adjustment allowance instead had a $300 debit balance, reaching $2,800 credit would require a $3,100 credit provision. Keep debit and credit signs visible; subtracting an unsigned balance can produce the wrong answer.

Reconcile gross and net AR as well as the allowance

For the same fictional period, opening gross AR is $60,000. Add $40,000 credit sales, deduct $19,300 ordinary collections and $700 write-offs, reinstate $200 recovered receivable and collect that $200. Closing gross AR is $80,000. Total collections are $19,500, including the recovery; do not deduct that recovery twice.

Opening net AR is $60,000 − $1,200 = $58,800. Add $40,000 credit sales, deduct $19,500 cash collections and $2,100 provision to get $77,200 closing net AR. A write-off against an existing allowance reduces gross AR and allowance together, so it does not by itself create a second net-AR loss in this model.

Keep approval, evidence and estimation separate

Support write-offs and recoveries with approved customer records. Reconcile the detailed customer ledger to the gross AR control, and the allowance schedule to its own control account. A customer promise is not collected cash; a write-off is not a cash payment. Document the estimate owner, review date and changes in assumptions.

Use the receivable workflow for invoice detail and the bad-debt expense guide for the event-by-event provision, write-off and recovery entries. The current-assets guide explains gross versus net presentation. Tax deductibility is a separate determination and is not established by an allowance entry.

html:
Bad debt expense recognizes a credit-loss provision under the selected accounting policy. A later write-off and recovery are different events. Under an allowance approach, do not record the same expected loss again as expense when the customer balance is removed.

All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies.

Identify whether you are estimating, writing off or collecting

This original example uses a US GAAP-style allowance approach for trade receivables, solely to explain posting mechanics. It does not build the full expected-credit-loss estimate. Opening gross AR is $25,000 and allowance is $1,500 credit. Assume a separately supported review requires a $900 current provision before the later events below; there are no other sales, ordinary collections, credits or tax effects.

The allowance guide owns estimation, including current FASB policy choices. A percentage of sales or a textbook aging table should not automatically be described as complete current US GAAP compliance. Keep the entity’s applicable method and approval evidence visible.

Record each event with its own balanced entry

Original allowance-method entries, USD
EventDebitCreditCash at this step
ProvisionCredit loss / bad debt expense 900Allowance 900None
Approved write-offAllowance 1,200Customer receivable 1,200None
Reinstate recovered balanceCustomer receivable 300Allowance 300None
Collect recovered balanceCash 300Customer receivable 300Receipt 300

The provision reduces current profit by $900 under this case’s expense convention. The write-off uses the existing allowance. Reinstatement restores the customer item before the supported receipt is allocated. Do not treat the recovered $300 as another sale or automatically reverse $300 of expense without examining the actual policy and allowance estimate.

A write-off decision requires documented authorization and the relevant accounting assessment. It is not created merely by reaching an arbitrary number of days overdue. Collection rights, customer communications and tax treatment can involve separate considerations.

Follow gross AR, allowance and net AR through the sequence

Original event-level balance bridge; no other movements
StageGross ARAllowanceNet ARCash movement
Opening balances25,0001,500 credit23,5000
Record 900 provision25,0002,400 credit22,6000
Write off 1,20023,8001,200 credit22,6000
Reinstate recovered 30024,1001,500 credit22,6000
Collect recovered 30023,8001,500 credit22,300+300

The $1,200 write-off reduces gross AR from $25,000 to $23,800 and allowance from $2,400 to $1,200, leaving net AR unchanged at $22,600. Reinstating $300 increases both balances and still leaves net AR at $22,600. Collecting $300 then changes the composition of assets: net AR becomes $22,300 and cash increases $300.

Across the full sequence, opening net AR $23,500 − $900 provision − $300 recovered cash collection = $22,300. The write-off is not a $1,200 cash payment, and the recovery is not $300 new revenue. Reassess the closing allowance under the actual reporting policy after all relevant evidence is considered.

Do not confuse an allowance provision with direct write-off treatment

A direct write-off presentation records an expense when a specific receivable is removed, rather than first using an allowance. That timing differs from the modeled sequence. It is not presented here as an unrestricted alternative for financial reporting or as automatic tax treatment. Method suitability, materiality, framework and current requirements need their own review.

Financial-reporting expense, customer-ledger removal and tax deduction can occur under different conditions. Recording an allowance or approving a customer write-off does not itself prove a tax deduction is available. This guide intentionally makes no deduction amount, eligibility or filing claim.

Reconcile and preserve the recovery trail

Retain customer ID, original invoice, provision policy, write-off approval, reinstatement reference, bank evidence and cash allocation. Check the customer subledger against gross AR and the allowance rollforward against its control account at the same cutoff. If a receipt cannot be identified, investigate rather than attaching it to a convenient written-off balance.

Use the collection workflow for payment matching, the general ledger record for posting references and the accounting cycle for the reviewed close. A clear audit trail keeps estimation uncertainty separate from an observed bank receipt.
